Grand Lodge of OoJ,ifornia.

Our annual meetings are communion seasons for the Craft, at which, by free 111·
terchange of thought, the variances of opinion which spring up in isolated communities are harmonized, reconciled, and adju~ted. The interchange of ideas here cul·
tivated promotes those fraternal feelings which, carried by the representatives to
their homes, grow more bright when reflected by the body of the Craft, imbuing
them with sentiments of virtue and charity, inculcating nobler thoughts and higher
aspirations, and making it a proud distinction to be known as a Mason. Let us not
f'orget, in our leglslati9n, tbat we are governed by landmarks which have stood immovable for centuries, and that we are but Interpreters, adapting them to the situa·
tion and wants of a pro;ressive age. Let us be grateful to b;e great Dispenser of all
Good for the prosperity vouchsafed to us during the past year, for the many
blessings we have enjoye.d, and for the general exemption from that dread decree
which man can not escape ; thus permitting us to meet so many familiar faces re·
fleeting the glow of health and happiness.
The general prosperit.Y. of the Craft throughout the jurisdiction Is gratifying.
Many new Lodges have been formed during the past year, and our membership Is
steadl!y Increasing ; thus giving our Order a promls~ of that future success sure to
spring from the Intellectual class now being admitted, who will hereafter teach and
Illustrate Its adaptability to Improve and elevate mankind •
With the various Grand Bodies of Mllsonry throughout the world our relations are
of the most friendly nature, our lnteroourse being marked with the oourtesy characteristic of the fraternal bond, But three 1nstances of vlollltion of our jurlsdiotiona! righb have been brought to my knowledge during the past year ; one by a
subordinate of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, and two by subordinates in the
State of New York. I informed the Grand Masters of those States thereof, who
promptly replied to my oommunlcations, and the Grand Master of New York imme·
diately suspended the offending Lodges until satisfactory explanation was made in
reference thereto. I have also received a communication from the Grand Master of
Masons in Tennefll!ee, acknowledging, In the most fraternal manner, the vlol11tlon of
jarlsdictlon to which _m y predecessor alluded in his annual address, explaining the
error of tht1 subordinate Lodge, and asking us to have the brother healed and allowed
Me.sonic rights.
During the past year I have granted twelve dispensations for opening new Ludges,
all, with one exception, being located In the agrloultural dl~trlcu of the State, where
their permanence and prosperity is unquestioned. I have also granted sundry apeolal
dispensations in cases provided for by the Constitution, the purposes of which w!!l be
furnished by the Grand Secretary in his report. Not being able to attend myself, I
Issued speolal authorizations for the dedications of halls ereeted and owned
respectively by LoB .Angeles"Lodge, No. 42, Texas Lodge, No. No. 46, and Woodland
Lodge, No. 156; and I also issned an authorization to th11 w... Bro.JOSEPH IBAAOB, to
le.y the corner-stone of a Methodist Episcopal Church In the town of Millville, In
She.eta County: all which duties we1e sat!sf&otorlly perfotmed by the brethren des·
ignated to discharge them. I refused permission to dedloate a ball owned In partnership with another organization which also Intended to perform a similar ceremo'
ny, not believing it In consonance with our teachings that hal!s dedicated to Masonry
should be dedicated to other purposes also.
Some amendments to the Constitution will in m'y opinion be advantageona, and
produce a g.ood effect. The fee charged for affiliation should be no longer demand-·
ed, as we require membenhlp, or application therefor, to place one in good standing, and at the same time affix thereto conditions which, in some instances, may
make it a hardship, or at least deter those who would otherwise make application,
from doing so. Membership in a Lodge is a duty which every Mason should fulfll, if
possible, and our laws should place no obstacle in the way which serves as an ex·
~
cnse for n·on-e.fl!!iatlon.

I also recommend that the law In 'reference to the ballot be made positive and
binding, requiring all Lodge1 to have but one ballot for the three degrees. Such is
now the rule of nearly all tbe Lodges, and I see no good reason why a rule that is
found to operate harmonlou1ly In one hundred and sixty.five Lodges out of one hundred and seventy, thou Id 'ee objectionable to the other five. I think that Sec. 7, Art.
III, Part III, of the Oon1tlt11tlon, 1hould be so amended as to require one half the fee
to accompany tire petition, the other half to be paid previons to initiation. As it
now reads It has been ml1under1tood In many instances, and it should be made plain.
I also recommend that the 4th and 7th General Regulations be repealed , and that
the 13th be amended. fhe 4.th Regulation I consider no longer necessary, for the
theory of material jurisdiction le so well understood and recognized by the various
Grand Lodges that a vi olation thereof can not well occur which will warrant the
form of condonatlon specified In that regulation. The 7th Regulation is no longer
necessary, as the cir11amstances which caused its adoption no longer exist. The 13th
Regulat~on should be so amended as not arbitrarily to fix the amount of tax levied
for the Representative Fund, but to conform to the practice of the Grand Lodge in
levying the amount necessary for each year.
At our last Annual Communication the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Hall
Fund were directed to Inquire Into and ascertain the ~ltuation of and interest held by
the Grand Lodge in the (so-called) GABS and CL.ABK property in Sacramento ; and
Bro. RICHARD DALE, of said Board, after making all Inquiries practicable, and finding that ·an attempt to recover the property would be attended with expensive and
protracted litigation and doubtful •access, after f\dvlsing with the officers of the
Grand Lodge and his co-Trustees, compromised the claim npon terms, in my opinion, greatly to the interest of this bod.v. His services in this matter should be appreciated by the Grand Lodge, for, without his assistance, in all probability nothing
would have been realized from that source.
In regard to the work, I learn that there is oonsiderable difference in practice
among the Lodges, and have come to 'the conclusion that the present system of its
attempted dissemination by an unpaid Grand Lecturer is not conducive of good result~.
The term of ten years would not be s.ufficient for one Grand Lecturer to visit all the
Lodges and correct their errors and at the same time teach all who desire to acquire
the work and lectures. I have no doubt that had the system practiced during the
years 1863-4-5~ been continned, there would have been no cause for complaint iii
regard to uniformity. A Grand Lecturer resident at San Francisco, or some convenient locality, and paid a sufficient 11alarjlfor devoting the time necessary to teach all
who desire to perfect and qualify themselves for teaching is, in my opinion, the only
way in which the work and lectures 'can be kept uniform, for theµ there is a fountain-head within reach of ail thirsty inquirers. It would be far better for the Craft
to abolish the office than to retsin it according to the present system. A Grand Lec'turer can not visit anrl instruct all the Lodges In persclh; and besides, many Lodges
prefer to have one of their own number become their teacher, the expense being
Iese than that incurred by the employment of a traveling Grand Lecturer. I hope·
the Grand Lodge will take some action to return to and re-ensure the uniformity once
before attained.
The appointment of Representatives near other Grand Lodges is a custom which
tends to preserve the harmony that should be maintained between Grand Bodies exercising independent authority, and it Is a gratifying acknowledgment of that fraternity of sentiment which is the distinguishing characteristic of Masonry. With these
views, and in reciprocation of the appointments made near our Grand Lodge, I hllve
accredited the following named distinguished Masone as our Representatives near
their respective Grand Lodges, viii!: for Tennessee, the R.·. W.·. TowNSEND A.

Again it is gratifying to note the fact that no surrender of a charter has occurred
during the year, as it is one of the evldenc~ of the Increasing stability pf everylhlng
.in ourSta.te. :While, f.<M"merly, every annual l'eport showed the exti11ction of one pr
more Lodge~, three years have now elapsed without such an occurrence, and with
the e)!:isti~ state of things, it iR not probable that hereafter the Grand Secr~tary
will be calletl npon ·often to record such an event. In tile earlier days dispensations
and charters were granted freely to our brethren in the mining gulches, but when
the gulch was worked out, so also was the Lodge, and thus mo.ny vacancies were
created in the nnmbers upon our registry. During the, fater years our popnlation has become mpre fixed, even in the mineral-bearing: portions of the State, as
quartz and hydraulic mining affords a far more permanent employment than the
placer washings of the early period; and in the agricultural counties, now rapidly
and' oonstantly filling with farmers who establish homes, where, during severlL\ years
paat, most of the Lodges have been instituted, there is little to 're.tr for their perma·
nence and usefulness.
'fhe numbers upon our register of chartered Lodges hnve now reached to one
hundred and ninety-two. Of these, twenty-one, for reasons heretofore presented,
have voluntarily surrendered their charters ; three have be<Jome extinct.by the revocation of those instruments ; two, established in Oregon, assisted in the formatiol}
of the Grand Lodge of that State ; arid, eight, instituted ln N evade., transferred their
allegiance to the Grand Lodge there esta.blish.ed ~themselves. Thus ihete are now
in' active existance within this jurisdiction one nnndred and fifty-eight· chartered
Lodges, besides the twelve to which dispensations have been issued since the last
Annual Oom111unlcat!on-mU:l111 in all one hundred and seventy.

At the last Annual Communication it was ordered that the portraits of Past Grand
Masters JAHEB J,, ENGLlSH, JONATHAN D. SrEVENBON, WtLLTA:I! H. HowARD, and
WILLI.AH A. DAVlEB, be procnred and placed among the other portraits int.he offices
of the Grand Lodge. In accordance with that order, soon after the close of the
Communication, the undersigned gave a direction for the pictures to Bro. STEPHEN H.
8HAW, the artist to whose skilful pencil the Grand Lodge is indebted for the life-like por·
traits already in its possession; and three of them-those of Bros. ENGLISH, STEVEN·
BON, and HOWARD-have been finished and are now presented. The fourth has not
been taken, becanse, as stated by the artist, he was unable to obtain the attendance
of Bro. DAVIES for sittings; but it is hoped that before leaving the city now, he will
find opportunity for that purpose.

, A.s these proceedings contain some seven or eight thousand pages of printed
matter, it woo Id be a surprising fact if your committee had succeeded In do(ng justice to all, or had called attention to all that was or would have been of general
interest. We only claim that we have done as well as we could. Our time bas not
at 1111 times b'een at our dlsposBI, and this report has been prepared at odd Intervals,
amid pre~lng avocations, which almost compelled us to throw up our appointment
and ask the Grand Master to name some more fortunate indivl.dual. But, such as It
ls, we now submit our report to the brethren of the Grand Lodge. Differing from
many of our cotemporarles, we do not think It the business of the CQmmittee on Correspondence to usurp . the functions of either Grand Master or Committee on Masonic
Jurisprudence. We have therefore purposely ltme but little in the discussion of
questions of Masonic law, and have carefully avoided setting ourselves up as the
"Sir Oracle" of the Order. Whenever an opinion has been expressed, the reader
will understand It as an individual utterance merely, and not Bn ex-cathedr.a decision of the particular question. Our aim has been to cull, from the many reports f
submitted to us, items touching the welfare and proceedings cif the severe.I juriediotlons, which were of interest to us, and, as we hoped, would also be to the members
of the Order In CaliforniB. With this preliminary explanation, we submit our work
for the Inspection of the Craft.

ALABAMA.
The forty-eighth .Annual. Communication of the Grand Lodge of Alabama was
held at Montgomery, commenclr.g December 7, 1868. The M.'. w,., G1110RGE D. NOR·
RIS presided as Grand Master, and the R.·. w,., DANIEL SAYRE was Grand Secretary.
Representatlvee'were ,present from two hundred of the two hundred and tlfty-four
working Lodges In this jurisdiction.
The Grand Master's address covers fifteen pages of the pamphlet of proceedings.
It is a well· written, able, thoroughly Masonic document, mainly taken up, as we think
all such e.ddreSBes should be, with matters of local Interest to the Fraternity in the
jurisdiction ; and we present a few of the pearl11 which we find lu its begitining :.In this world, where everything le transient and unsettled, we look with .peculiar
anxiety for something that Is permanent; we like to create objects which can survrve
the fleeting life of man; objects which, handed down from 11:eneration to generation,
ue reviv~d in eaoh succeeding race, and amid the mortality of the world,· catch an
immortality from the zeal and devotion of man. Such objects as these are tbe perpetual vehicle& of th.ought; they Impose upon both the same mystic bonds, and
weave the distantfort!ons of the human race together in one great family.
By the force o this fraternal connection, the antipathies of hostile nations are
overcome; patriotism brea.ks over the bounds of clime and language, and enlarges
until It embraces the world .
Loaded with the charms ofantlquity, interesting by a thousand asRociations of history, herol~m, and romance, the order yet possesses ail the health and life of novelty,
all the liberality and benevolence of reform. It exists In the body and bosom of the
people; it catches their sentiments, is modified by their thouglJts, and changes with
their manners. It partakes of their improvement, and adapts itself to a.II the various
changes of man. Within its shBdow the rich and the poor meet on terms of equality;

of your childhood to come here? The ready r esponse was: No, I will go back;
(and I trust every good man will come back ;) I will remain where I .am. I felt when
I returned home, as I feel here, standing in your midst to-day, that these are my
brethren; that this is my country; endeared by numb~rlcss r ecollections of the past,
and by the hopes of the future. ·rt is hallowed in my aft'e ction as the last resting
place of my kmdred, and I can truly say" r love its very dusts and aimda,

Question.-A Master Mason voted for the adoption of the Constitution nt the
late election: iR it a violation of Masonry or not?
·
Answer.-No. The p;ood brother who propounded this question, indicated in his
letter that some of the members of his Lodge, regarding the Constitution as proscrip·
tlve and unjust to a class of citizens of the State, among whom w.11.re Masons, were
reluctant to fellowship with the brother who voted for it, on the grll'und that he had
been heedless of' his relations to his brothers of the clnss proscribed, etc.
!Io matter what may be the character of the Constitution, its adoption or non·
11doptidn was •trictly a political question, with which the Lodges or Masons, as such,

admission, and at every step of his advan~ement, that Masonry does not Interfere
with his political or religious opinions, eto.; yet It is hard to educate human nature

.

with political and religious controvers1e1. Had Mason•, as suoh, pe.rticipated In the
political and religious disputes which have separa.ted men Into parties and sectsIed to bloodshed and persecution- and brought into the Lodges the prejudices, big·
otry, and Intolerance engendeMd by partiz110 strife, Masonry wo~ld have failed to
accomplish her great mis~ion of charity, been disintegrated, and' wrecked in ages
gone. Happily for frail and fallen humanity, Masonry, in her mission of mercy to m11n,
has erected an altar, around which she asoembles her children of all political opinions and religious creeds, and binds them together, as a hRrmonlous brotherhood, by
a cord that is not easily broken. Moreover, out of the Lodge, no matter how widely
my brother may ditfer from me on political opinions or religious subjects, if he be
hungry and I fail to feed him; naked, and I fail to clothe him . roofless, and I fail to
shelter him; sick, and I fall to minister to his wants; in peri1or danger, and I fail
to go to his 1'elief, 1 am no true Mason.

Our brethren of this well· known parallelogram State send us greeting, with the
proceedings of the eighty-first Annual Communication of their Grand Lodge, held in

The Address of the Grand Master is one of the ablest and best wrltt~n that has

Tile ffoances of the Grand Lodge were in a very unsatisfactory state, ow lug to

same.
The Grand Master commends to the favorable notice of the Craft the "Mason's
Mutual Benefit A1Jsoclatlon" of Hartford, and hopes that every Freemason In the
jurisdiction will secure the benefits of membership.
In conclusion, the Grand Master announces that he will not be a candidate' for reelection. He states the ft1ct that for twenty-six years he had been a permanent
member of the Glhncl Lodge, and had never been absent from 11 single Annual Communication.
3.'he Grand Lecturer submitted a report from himself and. his several Deputies,
which showed th.at none of the number had been idle or lazy during the year.
The Grand -Lodge treated rather gingerly the communication from Louisiana
(noted tinder: tlmt·iuiad) about the action of the " Grand Orient" of France, being
unable, as the· committee says, "from the papers in their banda, to obtain a complete history of the case." These resolutions, however, were adopted :Resolved, That In the opinion of this Grand Lodge, no organization, except the
Grand Lodge of Louisian11, has any authorlry or power to establish or c.ontrol Blue
Lodge$ in the State of Louisiana.
Hesolverl, '!'hat this Grand Lodge expresees the hope that the recognition of any
organization except the llrand Lodge of Louisiana, as having any authority or power
in or over Blue Lodges In the St11te of Louisiana, by the Grand Orient of France,
will be speedily rever•ecl.
Tho Jleport of the Committee on Oorre1pondence, as usual, la from the pen of
the worthy Grand Secretary. It Is an able ancl lntMestlng review of the prooeldings of thirty-nine Grand Lodges, our own for 18H8 being one. We copy this aentence from the opening paragraph, merely remarking, that they expreBB our sen ti·

ILLINOIS.
The proceedings of the twenty-eighth Annual Communication of this Empire
Grand Lodge of the Empire State of the Mis•issippi Valley, come to us in a hand·
somely-printed pamphlet of over two hundred and fifty pages. The sessions we re In
Springfield on the 6th and 7th of October, 1868,-the M.·. W:. JER0:\1£ R. GORIN pre:
sidlng as Grand Master,and the R.·. W:. HAR:l!A.N G. REYNOLDS being Grand Secretary.
Representatives were present from four hundred and thirty subordinate Lodges; and
we notice that upon one division, one thousand one hundred and twenty-six votes
were actually ca.st. How such a Grand Lodge can get through with all its business
in two days . as this one uniformly does, is a mystery to us on this Pacific coast.
In California we spe11d just half of that time in our elections, and yet five hundred
is about the maximum vote ever cast in our Grand Lodge. 0 ur brethren in Illinois
must be largely blessed with implicit faith in the fidelity and correctness of those entrusted with the management of the aft'alrs of the Grand Lodge, ot else must
possess a double portion of that spirit of brotherly love about which.,good King
David san~, and of which our Entered Apprentices first learn. Which is it, good
brethren ?- or are you blessed with both? Why, it took that little knot of fifty odd
vinegar-faced old women fa11atlcs, who rece11tly honored Chicago with their presence
and diatribes against Masonry and all secret societies, more than te11 days to get the
·bile off their stomachs, and then they were about as mnch jaundiced as ever.
The Address of the Grand Master was very brief Indeed. He simply tells the
Fraternity abont Illinois and what he had done, and leaves the rest of the world to
take care of itself, or be regulated by the "Little Pedlington" editors, of whom,
it, is quite clear, Grand Master GORIN is not one. He had issued during the year
thirty-six dispensations for the organization of new Lodges. The plan adopted for
the year, as an experiment, of dividing the State into twelve districts, each to be
under the supervision of a Depnty Grand Master, had, in the estimation of the Grand
Master, proved a success, and he recommended its continuance as a permanent
arrangement. The Grand Lodge concurred.
The subjeot of the speedy erection of a Grand Lodge hall was urged by the Grand
Master as one of great importance. He suggested that each snbordinate Lodge sub·
scribe or contribute stock to the amount of $300 on an average. This would produce
$180,000. A committee of the Grand Lodge, to which this matter was referred, reported the following resolution : Resol'Oed, That e very Lodge shall pay to the Grand Lodge the sum of one dollar
for each Initiation, each passing, and each raising in such Lodge, payable semi-annually on the first day of January and July in ea.ch yeo.r, and twenty-five cents for each

The Grand Master is very full in his discussion of the acts of the Grand Masters in
other jurisdictions, and in the expression of hia opinions on points of Masonic law and
usage, raised thereby. To some of these we shall briefly allude , without taking much
part In the discussion. For, as stated in our report last year, our aim Is not so
much the ostentatiou~ ventilation of our own wonderful Masonic wisdom or ignorance,
as the case might be, as to give our brethren of this Grand Lodge a running sketch of
what is being said and done by the Fraternity throughout the Union, and the world
at large, so far as we can ga.ther the same II-om the reports laid before the Committee.
We doubt not but that these will be of more interest than would be our own owl-like
lucubrations about "Ancient Landmarks " and "things of that sort." If our brethren , in this, differ from Ub, our pen, spectacles, and patience are at once placed at the
command of any brother who can, or thinks he can, do better.
The Grand Master discusses at some length the claims of the Grand Master of New
York, and of some others who agree with him, as to his right to " make Masons at
sight." The negative of that'posltlon ls a.b!y argued, Some strong points are taken,
and yet much appears to us to be special pleading. Very few principles, even; will
bear to be carried out to all conceivable lengths, without involving absurdity.
The Grand Master further maintains, that In all the proceedings of a Grand or
subordinate Lodge, not referring to work, there should be an appeal from the Master's decision to the Lodge. He conjures up. quite a spectre of what might happen,
under certain supposed circumstances, about which we are disposed to use his own
words on another point, viz: that" it is not a supposable case in a Masonic Lodge."
Having, In our half century of life, been tolerably familiar with the action of deliberative bodies, where appeals are.allowed on every point of dltrerence, as also with
Masonic Lodges, Grand and subordinate, where they are prohibited in all, we give the
decided preference to the last. Less mischief will be done in the long run, and much
better order and harmony1>reserved. We were much struck on the occasion of an
installation of Grand Officers, at the remark made by the Installing officer to the
Grand Master elect, as he presented him with the gavel: "This," said he , "is nn em·
blem and implement of authority which no brother dare disregard, and which no
Master or Grand Master dare abuse."
He maintains that" Lodges under dispenS'atlon," as ls the case in Indiana, should
have " all the rights and powers of chartered Lodges, except that of electing and in·
stalling the officers, holding public processions, and being represented In Grand
Lodge." In this view we fully concur, and such is substantially the law and practice
in CaliforQla.
'·
The old and almost time-worn questions, of "the power of· a Master or Warden to
resign "-the " status of army-made Masons "-of the "side degrees," .so called-and
the physical qualifications of candidates, are all discussed In this address, but we have
neither time nor disposition to follow tbe Grand Master in his wandering through suoh
fields, rich and promising as they may appear to others. The "Aft-loan" question is
also gently tone.bed, but in this the motto of the Grand Master Is ours: "Sufficient
unto the day is the evil thereof."

objects as beyond the necessity of mere defense. The institution is now presented to
the world with a growing confidence in the vitality and fruitfulne~s of its organic h111tory. It is better understood by Masons themselves, and is consequently presented
with greater distinctness, and with less seeming antagonism, and exclusiveness, and
zeal, without knowledge. Many who have looked with suspicion upon the Order, as
claiming more than can possibly pertain to any human institution; even the supplant;
ing of the necessity of anything outside of the Order, either for morality, religion, or
civilization, have found that Masonry as presented by her best, and ablest advocate ,
is the handmaid of all that is good , beautiful, and true, and not the exclusive owner of
the sunlight, the love, or the redeeming merits of that God, who binds to ilimself in
golden chains, the whole human family.
The object of Masonry is not the same as the Church or the Sta.Ui. It has a yeculiar mission of its own, and by the distinct preso,ntatlon of that mission, so that al may
see it, the less will be the suspicion in the world against the institution, und the more
plainly will its peculiar merits be manifested, and unfolded In fruits of beuuty, rich·
ness, and delight. Masopry is not a religious or a politic11l bod:y. Itis not exclusively
or primarily a teacher of morality or politics, in the sense of' practically applying the
moral principles of any religion, or the practical principles ot· any civil government;
but in common with all religions and all State autborit)', it starts with the fact of the
brotherhood of the human race; and believing that to think over problems tlutt relate
to action between man and man, without proceeding to act, is to become speedily
paralyzed; it acts, and its action Is a societr. The mysteries of' mutual, fraternal,
action do not yield up their secrets of light, while we
"8it apart, holding no form of Society,
But contemplating all."
The formative principle of Masonry finds its illustration In that principle of science
by which the most minute and apparently isolateu facts resolve themselves into systems ; these systems again are hound together in still willer systems ; complex laws,
as we ascend higher In the scale of being, unfold their complex operations and assume simpler forms. . And so we go from intlnite diversity to a higher 'anu higher
unity; until we find all reduced to 11 unity ot one universe, beneath the throne of one
God.
From tliis fundamental principle of science, springs the development of mind, in
the activity of thought, and the various applications of the conclusions gained.
In the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God, is the unity of one human
family; and this principle is the formative principle of Masonry. 'l'he realization of
this sublime fact developes obligations, moral, religious, and political. But Masonry
aims not at the presentment or enforcement of obligations abstractly considereu, only
at the inculcation of the family relationship, from which spring morality, religion,
civil obeuienco, and progress. Other organization ~ and instrumentalities, Divine and
human; have their legitimate phtce in the worlu 's history, to which Masonry claim~
only to be the handmaid, and from which Masonry welcomes light and truth, and all
elements that tend to the realization and perfection of the brotherhood that it is her
peculiar mission to insi~t upon, and illustrate;
"For so the who!~ r&und earth, is every way ·
Bound by golden chains, about the feet of Clod."

The opening address of the Grand Ma~ter is somewhat long, but a well written,
common sense, and able document. The writer had no reason to apologize in advance
for the" absence of the graces of Rhetoric." He evidently knows what he wants to
Aay, and when to say it, in good Anglo-Saxon English, and that is as good rhetoric as
Is to be found in Quackenboss, Blair, or anywhere else.
During the year he had granted dispensations for the formation of twenty-one new
Lodges. In each case, he tells us, he had "endeavored to satisfy.himself that the proposed Lodge was not only required for the accommodation and convenience of the petitioners, but that the good of Masonry would be promoted by granting their prayer."
In one instance, at the earnest request of a Worshipful Master, the Grand Master
had retired him from his office, appointed the Senior Warden Worshipful Master, and
another brother Senior Warden in place of the one promoted. We should consider this
as decidedly out of order in this jurisdiction, if not a plain violation of the " Ancient
Landmarks."
It is the old question of a Worshipful Master resigning or dimitting, under a new
phase, the right of which we question. But If, from any cause, a vacancy does occur,
then the Senior Warden succeeds by right of his office, being Worshipful Master pro
tern for the rest of the Masonic year. Where ditl the Grand Master flntl hill authority
for his action?
Several new halls had been dedicated during the year, and a number of corner
stones laid. "Schools of Instruction" had been held in several localities, the result of
which was favorable, though perfect unanimity in" work" had not been attained. He
warmly commends to Masonic patronage "The Evergreen," a monthly periodical, of
which our eccentric brother, Past Grand Master GUILBERT, is editor in chief. If the editorials have the spice and llavor of Bro. G.'s reports as Grand Master and Chairman
of the Committee on Correspondence, we hope a copy will be sent us semi-~ccasion­
ally. lt would help our digestion wonderfully, and drive otf any fit of the blues that
might threaten us.
Appropriate notice is taken of the death of Bro. JORN LocKWOOD CORSE, a Past
Grand Junior Warden, and one of the founders of the Grand Lodge of low-a zeal•
ous Mason and a good man.
These closing words of the Grand Master are so excellent and appropriate that we
copy them for the benefit of our readers:Let us remember that at the present time our every word and act are closely scrutinized by most active, vigilant and earnest enemies of Masonry, anxious for even a
straw on which to base their wicked, slanderous persecution~. Our best defense and
protection against their attacks is to purity our order by purging our Lodges of the unworthy, and car_efully guarding the outer door, so that none but those whose daily lives
are a guarantee ~honor and uprightness can gaip admission. The motives of each applicant should be closely scrutinized, and his character and standing carefully investigated. It is not enoui1h that no one knows any evil of him. He should possess positive
1md affirmative qualities of goodness and influence, such as tend to raise him in the
ice le of life. The external qualifications of " worldly wealth or honor" should never
be considered for a moment, when the internal qualifications of mind and heart, of
truth, honesty and uprightness before God and man, are wanting. The destiny of our
Institution rests entire I):' in the hands of the fraternity itsejf, and we have more to fear
from our own errors within than from the attacks of those without.

Abst1·act of Deci.'lions by the Grand Master, approved by the Grand Lodg~.
1. A brother cannot be a member of t1vo Lodges at the same time.
2. A brother cannot be an officer of a Lodge U. D. without a demit from a regular
Lodge.
~. A suspended Mason cannot be recognized while under that sentence, and no
Lodge has a right to receive his petition or initiate him again. He must first be re·
stored to all the rights .and privileges of' Masonry by the Lodge suspending him or by
the Grand Lodge of the State under whose .inri"<liction the same was held before he
can be allowed to affiliate or be recognized Musonically.
'
4. Desertion trom the military service of the United States is not a Masonic crime
'
which should subject a brother guilty thereof to trial and discipline by his Lodge.
5. A Lodge opened in the absence of the W.·. M.·. and both Wurdens would be
clandestine, and all work done therein would be Illegal and void.
6. The jurisdiction of a Lodge cannot extend beyond the State line, especially if
the adjoining State has a Grand Lodge of its own.
7. Charges can be !?referred in a subordinate Lodge against a former W.·. M.·,
offences committed while he waa W.·. M.·. of said J,odge, and he be tried and disciplined
therefor, provided the acts complained of were for gross unmasonlc conduct and not
of an official character.
'
8. The good standing of 1/- F.·. O.·. applying for advancement, and being rejected
ls not atf~cted ihereby; and he may renew his application at any subsequent stated
commumcatlon.
9. It is not necessary for a W.·. M.·. of a Lodge U. D. to receive the so-called P.·.
M.·.'s degree.
10. The officers of a Lodge U. D. need not be Installed before acting.
11. 'l'he fact that a man, otherwise fully qualified, is hair-lipped, and speaks his
words with difficulty, does not disqualify him from being made a Mason provided "his
articulation is sufticiently distinct to make himself known as a Mason.'"
12. Aft.er 11. candidate has been accepted and received the degrees of E.·. A.·. and
F. ·. G. ·., a brother li'om another LOd[Je protesting against his further advancement,
and refusing to give any reasons for his protest, held that the Lodge bad a riitht to disregard that protest, and that it was the duty of a brother protesting to put the Lodge
In possession of' all the facts in the case.
13. A visiting brother has no rigl1t to object to the Initiation of a candidate who has
been regularly elected. To permit that would be equivalent to conferring the right of
the ballot upon the visiting brother.
14. A W. ·. M. ·. has the right to order the Secretary not to write down certain portions of the testimony given in a Masonic trial, it' such testimony might tend to disclose
to the profane such thin11s as are "improper to be written."
15. A brother preferrmg cher(les Is a competent witness In the case. Any Interest
that may attach to his position will go to his credibility only.
16. A brother on trial for unmasonlc conduct has the right to impeach a witness
even if he be a member of his own Lodge.

The thirteenth Annual Colllfnunlcation of the Grand Lodge of Kansas was held in
Lawrence, October 20, 1808. irhe M.·. W:. M. 8. ADAMS presided as Grand Master,
anti the R:. W:. ERASlllUS T. CAUR was Grand Secretary.
'f he Address of the Grand Master is a brief, business-like document, and is mainly
taken up with local matters. He had granted dispensations for the formation of nine
new Lodges. It appears that the wandering and often-rejected brethren at Salt Lake
have at Inst found a home or resting-place, Kansas having taken them under her sheltering wings. It will be remembered that our Nevada brethren positively refused a
charter, and so ditl the Colorado or Montana Grand Lodge, we forget which. The
application having been made last year to the Grand Master of Kansas, he granted a
fupensation, having, as be says,"" no means of knowing whether the applicant@ were
the same or different brethren from those who made application to the Ur11nd Master
of Nevada." He now referred the whole matter to the Grand Lodge of Kansas for Its
consideration. The "Committee on Warrants" made a report thereon, which we copy
at length, as the Grand Lodge approved the s11me, and granted a charter.
"Your Committee on Warrant.R beg leave to re110rt that they have had under con·
sideration the application ol the brethren of Mt. Moriah Louge, U. D., at Great Salt
Lake City. They flntl the minutes of this LodlJe are correctly kept, the returns correct,
and that the By-Law• conform to our regulatwus. Objection~ to the establisment of
this Lodge have been raised by the Grand Lodge of Nevada, and their objections we
would not wi•h to wilfully disregard. Tltc brethren petitioning for a charter promise
a faithful adherence to our rule• and regulations, and several of them were formerly
members of this jurisdiction, and brothers who we believe to have the true Interest.I
of the fraternity at heart, and who would z eal ou~l y labor to promote the genuine prin·
ciples of' Freemasonry. The dlspensll'tion was granted to the brethren (wherein, per·
bttps, lays the only error 11nder the ciroumstances,} they have served their probation,
their work is approved, and with all du~ reference to the Hrand Lodge objections, we
would recommend that a charter be granted them."
·
Grave questions of Masonic law and comity necessarily attach to this·action of the
Grand Master and Grand Lodge of Kansas. But as it is not our funeral, and us Bro.
TAYLOR, of Nevada, is abundantly able to wield the sword in his own defence and that
of his Grand Lodge, we turn over the whole matter to him .
Having "for good and sufficient rettsons" granted some eleven special dispensations, the Grand Master gives some equally good ones why such should be very
sparingly granted. We concur in the preaching rather than in the practice.

Abstract of De<Mions !ly the Grand Master.

ihe State.
3. A Mason who has never served as Warden in a Lodge is not eligible to the office
of W.:. M." except in the case of a new Lodge.
4. A Lodge U. D. has no aathority to try a brother, whether affiliated or not.
5. There is no precise age fixed to limit the qualifications of candidates for the de·
grees of Masonry. The candidate must be in possession of the ordinary physical anp
mental faculties of perfect manhood.
KENTUCKY.
The proceedings of the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky,
held in Loui~ville, October 21, 1867., came to u~ in a B(}mewhat bulky volume of nearly
five hundred pages. The M .'. W.·. I. T. MARTIN preiided as Grand Master, and the
R.·. W.·. JoHN M. S. McCoRKLE was Grand Secretary. Representa,tives were present
from three hundred and seventeen subordinate Lodges.
The Address of the Grand Master is very brief, and is mainly confined to a state·
ment of the business transacted by him during the year. Here are some judicious sen·
tences which we copy from the opening page. They are suggestive to the Craft every·
where :" The year now drawing to a close has been one of unexampled activity among the
Craft, and our numbers have. been added to with fearful rapidity. We have been led
to look with alarm upon this rapid increase. This is not a democracy; not intended
for the million ; but for a select body of men, gathered up from the masses because of
their high moral worth and integrity of character. Men, among whom all can feel
that in each of this band he has a f'nend and brother, on whom he can lean wi.th the
fullest confidence. It should be the duty of every Mason to see that no one enters the
door at our Mystic Temple unless he be a man, in the full Masonic acceptation of the
term. It should be remembered too by every Mason that when the man is admitted
to our Order, that he not only becomes his brother, but the brother of every other
Mason also. We do not want numbers; the,r already encircle the world. Then why'
add a link to our chain unless it is a golden !wk? We really do not want money, and
If we do, can we af'!ord to barter away the privileges of our sacred order? Let us
then, brethren, guard well the outer door of our Mystic Temple."
The Grand Master goes after the non-affiliated drones in the Masonic hive with a
sharp stick. He suggests the adoption of some elfective remedy. Suppose, worthy
brother, you try a dose of our California medicine? We have this provision In our
Grand Lodge Constitution:"It is the duty of every Master Mason to be a member•of some Lodge ; and every
one who, having resided six months within the jurisdiction of a Lodge, shall refuse or .
neglec t to make application so to be, or who shall not have regularly contributed to
such Lodge an amount equivalent to its regular dues, while able so to do, shall be
deemed unworthy of Masonic consideration, and shall not be entitled to, nor be the
recipient of any of the rights, privileges or charities of the Order."
We have some of these drones in our midst, notwithstanding this stringent provis·
ion. But it has had a marked elfect in reducing their number as near to a minimum as
we can expect to attain in this Imperfect world of very fallible men. Our experience
having proved the inefficacy of moral lectures once a year from the Grand Master's

[Oct. 13,

favor of his view 11 weighty, and was as strongly presented in our Grand Lodge
by some of the oldeet and best members. But the decision, though not unanimous,
was emphatic. As we voted and argued in favor of the report of the commjttee, it
is proper to state that It was by no means intended to fix a stigma on the memory or
family of an unfortunate suicide, whether insanity was or was not the cause of the
act. But as facts were brought to light, showing what a disturbing element the fre·
quent discussions and decisions of this vexed question were in the several Lodges, it
was thought best to make an Iron rule, so that neither Masons nor the friends would
ask for a Masonic burial with all the funeral honors, thus declaring, almost with
mockery, that "the wlll of God was accomplished, and so mote it, be." It was
thought th~t Masons, as men and as sympathizers, conld show all needed attention
to such cases, both at the grave and elsewhere, without the enactment of that
mockery. We think the arguments of the committee on this subject were not only
cogent but una.nswerable, and we are glad· that our Grand Lodge took the decided
position
it did.

1. A Lodge may entertain charges against a suspended Mason, in cases where ez.

5. Where a Lodge grants a dimit to a member, his connection with that Lodge is
severed from that date. He can regain his membership therein only by a petition and
unanimous ballot.

eJ:istence. During that trying period, Bro. HERRING proved himself equal to thEj
emergency. He nobly and firmly met the combined attacks of fanaticism and perse·
cution hurled against ns by our furious and unprincipled adversaries. Many who

purified, and he lived to encourage the brethren until the Fraternity had reached a

Decided that a Warden , having served up tot.he annual election next after the reception of the warrant, is eligible to the mastership, then or at any future time; and

8. When permission is asked by one Lodge to. initiate a candidate previously rejected in another, is it necessary to have such permission before the candidate i~

• It is for the consenting Lodge to decide, when and nnder what circumstances they

9. A brother from a Lodge in Wisconsin, fourteen years in arrears to that Lodge,

this jurisdiction. Do thei>e circumstances all'ect his standing here ; if so, how?
The brother having failed to sever his connection with another jurisdiction, has
never lawfully come under this, and is therefore not a member of the Lodge.

Let us be reverently thankful to the Giver "of all good that we are enabled to
assemble in peace, love and unity, with none to molest us or make us afraid, and thus
to open and hold our convocation with pub.ic notice in open day, without the previous consent, and without the fear of any power, potentate or Rovereignty whatever,

Let us be thankful that our dwelling-place is in a land of civil and rellgiouB freedom, \Vhere we are blessed with that "perfect law of liberty " whieh our Father

No on.e who has carefully observed the signs of the pres~nt, indicatlnit difficulties
and dangers to the Frater11fty in the future , can have failed to be satisfied that the
rapid 111ultipllcatlon of Lodges ls one of the greatest perils that Masonry, from itll
almost certain consequences, has to fear. It necesstft'ily invites a great rush e.t the
threshold, wliich the new Lodge has neither the experience nor the nerve to resist.
The knowledge they have not, for that is only obtained by age and observation; t he
nerve they re.rely or never exercise, as they are compelled to meet large expenses
necessarily arising from the opening of a new Lode , the construction or fitting up a
hall, the procuring the insignia and jewels, the payment of the Grand Lodge fee, and
the thousand other items, often groRsly extravagant, but thought to be necessary,
to compe te successfully with the established Lodges in their vicinity. The new
Lodge is desirous of a large roil, of an elegant hall. of a full tree.Rury, and Is too for·
getful that these good things, in t hemselves, may be obtained at the loss of the permanent welfare and prosperity of \he Craft. By the gratification of these deslre1
they are prevented from exerllising that just discrimination and careful scrutiny BB
to petitioners for the d~grees, absolutely essential to the securing suitable material
for the Masonic temple, proposed to be constructed by the new r.odge. The certain
result is sure to follow, and the temple under con1truction is erected of roul!h stone.1,
a.nd put together with untempered mortar, the true work of Masonry lost sight of or
, neglected, and that temple which, had It been erected of good materials and In a
proper manner , would have stood as an enduring monument of the faithful labor& of
its founders, is soon levelled with the dust of the earth, and the "place which once
knew _it shall know _it no more forever. " There have already many such Lodges been
orgamzed, worked m this manner, and they are struggling for life, or have died;
enough to show plainly how dangerous is the path we have troddea ; enough stand-.
ing as grave-stones of Masonry-monuments marking the sloughs into which the Craft
·
have falle n from the errors of the past.

A new feature seems to be engrafted upon the proceedings of the Grand Lodge.
By resolution, the Grand Master is to detail one of the Grand Chaplains to deliver an
address at the opening of each Annual Communication, "not to exceed twenty min·
utes in length." The duty this year was devolved on Rev. Bro. F. C. EWER, formerly
a resident and well known clergyman in San Francisco. The address. is published at
length, and, as all who know the brilliant orator might expect, is a document well
worth reading and pondering. It is a stirring exhortation to the brethren to be "up
and doing," in some way worthy of their principles and ability. But if our good
friend and brother will permit us, we will ask if his ardent love for old style words,
only to be found in "Webster's Unabridged,'' is not sometimes apt to confuse the
ideas of his listeners and readers? For instance, in this paragraph, where did Bro.
EWER pick up the sentence we have marked in italics?How is it, sir, in other departments? Trade has its palaces; the Holy Church
hath her spacious and lordly structures ; the State has its schools, its capitols, its
hospitals, its treasuries; Art has its glyptoteks; Science has its halls, its observe.to·
ries, its gymnasia, its universities. But here is vast and compact Masonry without a
single structure that it can call its own, on the walls of which are emblazoned the
words·" Love to all Mankind;" not a hospital, not a medical school lookinp; to the alleviation of suffering, not an insane asylum, not a single training school for nurses,
not a roof for helpless age, not even a homely bunk into which the poor broken·down
sailor may crawl away from the great storm of life.
The whole address is so good that our brother wiil excuse this perhaps hypercrit.
ical comment.

of your Council, and approved under your hand, appear to h11.ve b~en: "To make
Masonry serve the purpose of introducing into the customs of the'peofle, so refractory on that point in the United States, even in the North, that civi and political
equality recently proclaimed between the white and colored races."
The report then states certain proceedings had by Lodges acting under that
Council to effectuate these objects, and proceeds: "In thus acting, this portion bf
the Masonic O~der in Louisiana followed t.he examples and practiced the principles
of :E'rench Masonry." This allegation is then sought to be established by the proceedings of the Louisiana Council, and the report in " consequence of the above
consideration," recommend" the favorable consideration of the proposal for recognition.
The Grand Master of Masons in New York understands from the above recital,·
that the Grand Oriept of France desires to make use of Masonry to introduce into
the United States certain political principles of equality between the white and
colored races; and for that purpose, among others, has given its Masonic recognition
to what is universally considered among the Grand Lodges of the United States to
be an unlawful Masonic organization, and the purposes to be eflectuated thereby as
entirely foreign to Masonry.
This communication is written for the purpose of remonstrating In the most fraternal.and respectful manner, not only again~t the· recognition of tbiR unlawful Conn· •
cil, but against the purposes and objects or that recognition, and to request that the
.
decree of recognition may be recalled.
It is further stated in the report which has been quoted, that the Grand Council
you have recognized " has completed its work b{ granting a charter to some colored.
men to open a Lodge and confer the degrees o Masonry, and that recently three
other Lodges have been formed by that Council of like material.''
The political objects sought to be accomplished through this recognition are entire!'- foreign to symbolic Masonry as conferred in the United States under its re~n­
lar Grand Lodges. No interference in political matters is allowed, nor any politics
discussed in our Masonic Lodges.
Not only is there no law of Masonr1 forbidding colored men from being :tnade
Masons, but our Lodges are exclusive Judge& as to whom they will accept, not violating the ancient landmarks; and colored mea may be members of Lodges, pro·
vided they are duly accepted. Bat they m'llst apply to lawfully warranted Lodges,
otherwise they are clandestinely made, and will not be acknowledged by· Mason)
or received in any regularly constituted Lodge.
'
The leading object, therefore, sought to be accomplished by the dec~ee will

This letter, as well as a previous one, written on the same subject by a member
of this Committee, has remained without answer or notice of any kind, and we are
irresistibly led to the conclusion that the Grand Orient proposes to stand by its decision, and to place a higher value upon the friendship of an irregular and clandestine
llSsor,iation than upon that of the regular Grand Lodges, which have so long been Its
allies and co-laborers in the cause. In thus acting, the Grand Orient decides not
only to approve the violation of our rights of jurisdiction, but invites a similar
trenching upon its own prerogatives and the breaking down of all legitimate Masonic
government. While we most sincerely regret this conclusion on the part of the
Grand Orient of France, and are pained in being forced to adopt the coutse of action
thereby indicated for us, duty to ourselves and to the great brotherhood of American
Grand Lodges requires that we should hesitate at no ·sacrifice necessary to de·
monstrate our unalterable determination to maintain intact the doctrine, that the
right of jurisdiction is inalienably vested in the •several Grand Lodges, and we therefore recommend the adoption of the third r esolution appended to this report.

NORTH CAROLINA.
The Eighty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of North Carolina
was held in the city of Raleigh, December 7-10, 1868. The M. •• w,., R. W. BEST pre·
sided as Grand Master, and the R.'. W.·. DONALD W. BAIN was Grand Secretary. Rep·

The Address of the Grand Master is a well written document , of moder11te length,
and mainly devoted to the consideration of local topics and the numerous decisions
he had been called upon to make during the year. He deprecates the untoward in·
fluence of bitter political feeling which had crept Into and disturbed the harmony of
some of the Lodges, and yet he commends the liberal use of the black ball, trµthfully
remarking that" Masonry Is not elevated by numbers. A few good and true Masons in
a Lodge are worth more to the Institution than a hundred drones and mischief-makers,
and if the black balls were brought more into use it would result in good."
He devotes considerable space to the ''Atevenson work" (whatever that may be),
which had been adopted by- the Grand Lodge, but had become somewhat mixed. not
to say muddled,-by the "original Jacobs," Father STEVENSON himself. The Grand
Lodge tried to straiten out the matter, and succeeded°, we believe, to its ·satisfaction.

OHIO.
The Grand Lodge or Ohio held lte fttty-nlnth Annual Communication at Dayton,
October 20-23, 1868. The M:. W.•. How.1.s11 MATTllll:W8 presided as Grand Master, ·
and the B.·. w,., JOHN D. CALDWlliLL was Grand Secretary. Representatives were
present from two hundred and sl:!:ty·ll.ve subordinate Lodges.
The Address of the Grand Master is quite elaborate, occupying more tban twenty
pages of the proceedings before us. He announces the gratifying fact that "an unprecedented degree of harmony and consequent prosperity had prevailed among the
subordinates during the year." He had issued dispensations for the formation of
twenty new Lodges.
·
Orie Lodge not only refused to notice and respect 11 written protest of 11 member
against conferring mor~ degrees on two Entered Apprentices, but ordered the same
to be laid "uuder the table," and proceed to confer the degrees. The Grand Master
very properly arrested the charter, and recommended that it be declared forfeited.
The Grand Lodge approved his action, but in consideration of the fact. that the
above was the act of but very few members, and contrition having been expressed,
the charter was restored.
He brings before the Grand Lodge the fact that relief had been extended to some
Ohio brethren by the San Francisco Board of Relief, and recommends that that body
should be reimbursed for the same.
Here is 11 suggestion that certainly appeals to one's sympathies as 11 man ancl 11
Mason. For one, we can see no strong objection to the course recommended, and
think that all Grand Lodges might thus provide for the intellectual welfare of its old,
but often pecuniarily unfortu.n ate brethren :We have among us 11 large number of those who have been active and zealous
Masons in other days, when blessed with health and vigorous manhood-who were
ever unremitting in the discha~ge of their. duty-yet now ~heir ent'ee.bled framAs and
tottering limbs prevent them from attendmg Lodge meetmgs, or enJoylng the pleasures of Lodge fellowship. They cling to their early love of the Institution, yet feel
that they have earned a respite from the burdens of the Lodge. As 11 t~ken of appreciation for the faithful service, I suggest that the subordinates be permitted to confer
on all who have been active members of some Lodge in this jurisdiction for a period
of twenty-one years, the title of" Emeritus Members,"relieving all such, during life,
from the payment of dues and assessments, and continuing them in the en~oyment of
all Lodge privileges; and that for all members certified to be" Emeritus,' no Grand
Lodge dues shall be charged. Honorary membership to remain as it is-'being conferred only on Masons who have rendered valuable service to the Institution, not active members of the Lodge conferring it.

A committee appointed to repQl"t a plan for" Special Masonic Relief," submitted
the following, which lies over for consideration at the next Annual Communication.
It adopts substantially the half-way Life Insurance policy which has recently become
so popular with our fellow-citizens. In theory all appears well, and we sincerely
hope that actual practice will not disappoint its advocates:RPBolved, 1. It is hereby recommended to the several f,odges in this jurisdiction
that they severally adopt and take measures to carry out the plan of special Masonic
relief proposed in this Grand Lodge , substantially as follows:1. Each brother agreeing thereto shall pay to the Secretary of his Lodge the sum
of one dollar and a half, and have his no.me registered in a book kept for the purpose,
together with the name of his wife, or if the brother be single, with the name of the
person be desires .to receive the benefit.
2. The money thus collected by the Secretaries of Lodges, shall be transmitted to
the office of the Grand Secretary, to be a fund of special Masonic relief, according to
the present plan. One be.If dollar of each first payment shall be appropriated to the
purchase of stationery and other needed expenditures.
3. On the death of a brother whose name is registered as aforesaid, the Secretary
of his Lodge shall notify the Grand Secretary of the fact, together with the name and
address of the widow, or other beneficiary, accompanying his communication with
the seal of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary she.II thereupon transmit to the widow
or beneficiary the funds collected from the several Lodges, excepting that retained,
as aforesaid, for necessar7 expenditures.
. 4. On being notified o the death of a member of the relief fond, the Grand Secretary shall communicate the fact to the Lodges of this jurisdiction which may have
adopted the plan proposed, and the Secretaries of these Lodges shall notify the brethren.
6. Each brother notified of the death of a member, shall, within two weeks, pay to
the Secretary of his Lodge one dollar, to be forwarded to the Grand Secretary as in
the case of the first payment, to form a fund for the relief of the widow or other de·
pendent of the next brother who may be co.lied away by death, in the same manner
as hereinbefore stated. Any member of this relief fund failing to pay when notified
of the death of a brother, shall cease to be a. member, and can only be reinstated by
renewing his membership, according to Article I, of this plan.
6. The Secretary of each Lodge adopting this plan of special Masonic relief shall
be entitled to retain three per cent. , and the Grand Secretary two per cent. of the

Abstract of Decisions.
1. No person can be initiated, passed or raised in this jurisdiction who is unable to
read an<! write, as every applicant must sign bis petition in his own handwritin¥·
2. A Lodge under disp.ensation has aut hority to enter, pass and raise candidates
only. It cannot affiliate members upon dimits.
S. A brother must have sat in ope .1 Lodge with another within one year, before he
can properly vouch for him ; otherwise he should be examined.
4. No Worshipful Master, Senior Warden, or Junior Warden caa resign or dimit
after conseuting to an election by being installed, ootil the expiration of his te1·m of
office.
•
o-. On the prese1!tation of e. petition for the degrees or affiliation, a vote should be
taken on its reception, and the vote must be unauimous Jn orderto lnsure its reference
to a committee.
6. No brother can be installed Worshipful Master of a subordinate Lodge in this
jurisdiction until he shall have received the Past Master's degree.
7. A Worshipful Master, Senior or Junior Warden of a subordinate Lodge In this
Jurisdiction canuot be a petitioner for a new Lodge during their term of office.
8. A petition for the degrees, after having been received and referred to a committee, ca nnot be withdrawn.
9. Every brother who receives the third degree in a subordinate Lodge beMmes
a member of the Lodge that confers it, unless by special request the work.is done for
another Lodge.
10. A Lodge can compel any non-affiliated brother within its jurisdiction to pay
dues, and if he refuse or fail to do so, can indefinitely suspend him; provided he has
not applied for membership and been rejected.
11. Any non-affiliated Master Mason who refuses to contribute the usual yearl1
dues to the Lodge under whose jurisdiction he resides, shall be deprived of the pri·
vilege of joining in Masonic processions, of receiving assistance, and of Masonlc
burial.
12. A Lodge cannot b"e opened for the transaction of any business in the absence
of the Master and both Wardens, except by the Grand Master or his Deputy.
13. ln the absence of the Worshipful Master the Senior Warden presides; and In
the absence of Master and Senior Warden, the Junior Warden presides, who has the
power to confer degrees and transact any other business as the Master might do if
present.
14: Any member of a Lodge In this jurisdiction who1e name has been stricken ·
from the r oll for non·payment of clues, reinstates himself by making payment.
·
15. Every Maeon who refuses to obey the summons of a Lodge of M11.ster Masons,
or its Worshipful Master, whether he be a member or otherwise, commiWI an otfense
against Masonry which demands stringent discipline.
16. A candid11te who has been irregularly made a Mason by a Lodge In good
1tanding, cannot be decla1·ed a clandestine made Mason, or refused the rights and
benefits of the Order; be not being held rc8ponsible for the improper act of the
Lodge that Initiated him.
•
17. The Worshipful Master has the right to place either of the Wardens or a
brother from the floor in the East, and permit him to confer either or the degrees
after having opened his Lodge •
18. A Lodge cannot deprive an accused brother of counsel when the report
.iomes before the Lodge for final action, provided the counsel la a Master Mason Jn
good standing.
19. Where a c&ndidate is a seafaring man and resides on bis vessel and has no
fixed permanent residence, he may make application for the degrees of Masonry to
any Lodge located at any port to which he may sail after t welve months.

The Committee on Grievances submitted this report, touching the rig.ht of a nonaffiliated Mason to a Masonic burial. A certain Worshipful Master had decided ln
the affirmative, from which an appeal was taken, and as will be seen, an adverse position taken. The committee are undoubtedly right as to the general principle, but
cases will sometimes occur, where the enforcement of such a rnle would be cruel in
the eirtremc, and in so far nnmasonic. Bot this is a question for each Grand Lodge to
decide for itself. We are glad to see that this committee makes room for such ex..
ceptional cases : We are glad that this question is presented for the decision of the Grand Lodge.
When a member of a Lodge, in good standing, dies, It Is the dnty of the Lodge, id
whose jurisdiction the death occurs, at the request of the deceased, or upon solicitation of his family or friends, if it can be dune with convenience, to accompany hjs
corpse to the place of interment, and there deposit it w.ith the usual formalities of
the Order. But your committee do unhesitatingly declare it is their opinion that it
is improper, as a general rule, for a Lodge to accord Masonic burial to a deceased
non-affiliated Mason. When a Mason voll}ntarily ostracises himself from the Order,
and seeks to relieve himself from the active duties and responsibilities of Masonry, ·
by withdrawing his membership from the Lodge, he Is not entitled, upon his demise,
to demand Masonic sepulture. But Masters of Lodges may, in certain cases, use
their own discretion as to buryinit deceased non-affiliated brethren, regnla.ting their
conduct, in all cases, by the 21st Section of Chapter V, Article 5th, of General Rules

(}rand Lodge of Cal.ifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred a question proposed by the Master of
Temple Lodge, No. 14, In which he asks the decision of the Grand Lodge In the fol·
lowing issue between his said Lodg~ and Hermann Lodge, No. 127, report as fol·
lows :Temple Lodge receive• the petition of a candidate, and, having elected him to
receive the degrees, conferred upon him the degree of Entered Apprentice. Upon
discovering his difficulty in acquiring the ritual, owing to the fact of his Inability to
entirely forsake his mother tongue, which Is German, at his own request Temple
Lodge "recommended" him to Hermann Lodge, In order to receive the degrees of
Fellow Craft and Master Mason, and for that purpose gave him an official document,
duly signed and sealed. With this he petitioned Hermann Lodge for the remaining
degrees, was elected, and was passed and raised in that Lodge. Temple Lodge now
wishes to be advised as to which of the two Lodges ls entitled to the fee for the work
done by Hermann Lodge.
The document submitted to us cannot be construed in any other light th~n as a
relinquishment of jurisdiction by Temple Lodge-a simple permission to Hermann
Lodge to confer the remaining degrees. It has no qualification which bears the
least appearance of an intention by Temple Lodge to ask the favor of Hermann!
Lodge to do the work for them which they could not satisfactorily complete ; but
the Entered Apprentice is certified as having been regularly Initiated, and is recom·
mended to Hermann Lodge for the remaining degrees.

To the M... W.·. Grana I..odae of Gmifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Addre88 of the Grand
Master relative to balloting for the degrees and the amount of fee which shall ao·
oompaoy ao aJllllication to be made a Mason, respectfully report that they do not
fc.el authorized to recommend the amending of the ConstitU)ion so as to make the
one bal~ot for the three degrees compulsory; bellevlng that a too frequent change
In that 1Dstrument could only r~sult io confusiou and injury to the Craft.
As to the other point, however, (that of the fee to accompany the petition ) they
nre of the opinion that the snbject is already fully provided for in Sec. 7, ~t. III
Part III, of the Constitution, which says: " in every case the fee for each, or all of
th~ degre~~· as ~ay be ~egulated by the Lodge, shall accompany the appllcation."
Tins provision, m the mmds of your commit.tee, is susceptible of but one construe·
tlon, evidently having been framed to accommodate the two modes of ballot prevl·
ously provided for. The words" fee for each," above quoted, have reference only to
Huch Lodges as may ballot for each degree separately ; and the words " all of the
degrees," apply to, and are imperative upon. all Lodges having but one ballot.
The conclusion necessarily follows that the fee for alt the degrees mu.~t accom a·
ny the application, except in cases where a: separate ballot is had for each degreep '
.All which is respectfully submitted.

7b the M. ·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the ap,peal of WESLEY STEVENSON from
the action of Gravel Range Lodge, No. 59, in sentencing him to be suspended from ·
all the rights and privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration arid
respectfully report that ihe charge against the accused is that he was g1iilty of false
hood. Truth is one of the virtues inculcated in Masonry. "T-0 be good and true is'
the first les•on we are taught"; but, at the same time, tliat which has been confided
to one as the secret of another can not be revealed without dishonor. From the
many contradictions to be f~und.in the testimony in this case and in the case of J. G.
MCLELLAN, with which it is intimately connected, your committee are in doubt as to
the real facts ; but, from a critical examination of all the testimony before the{n
bearing>upon the case, they believe 1hat if the accused was guilty of falsehood, he
could not have told the truth without revealing that which had been communicated
to him a3 the secret of another, and which he had promised to keep secret. Your
committee consequently find that the Commissioners erred in their judgment, and·
recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resoloed., That the action of Gra·oel Ran.ge Lodge, No. 59, in sentencing WESLEY
STEVENSON to be suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be re·.
versed and set aside, and that the charge be dismissed.
·
All which is respectfully submitted.

wisdom-the impersonations oftempernnce, courage, self-sacrifice, heroic suffering for
conscience' sake-the very types of simple, holy, earnest life. How different the

living tie life he preached, practicing the sublime precepts he taught-how different
when compared with the bedizened regalia and the glittering jewelry that adorn the
pompous persons of those rejoicing in their new degrees, their high-sounding titles of

Let no humble brother of tho blue Lodge distrust the fact that all of Masonry is
contained in the three ancient degrees, with the iustructions of the Royal Arch, nor
let him become envious ot' those wbo claim to be his superiors in Masonic knowledge
because they have had affixed to them, by some dignitary of the Order, the appella·
tion of "Thrice Puissant Grand Master," "Most Skillful Adoniram, " " Thrice Illustrious .A.zarias," Prince President," " Most Illustrious Tirshatha," "Very Wise Master,"" Thrke Pui•saot Chief Prince," " Most Potent Leader," "Sovereign Prince,"
or " Sovereign Grand Commander " ! Well has a standard writer upon Masonry remarked, that Wi1en theBe titles appear in the public prints they are only calculated to make the vulgar stare, and, with the right-feeliug, sensible Mason or man of
the worid, excite only derision and contempt.
L
But I must no\ permit myself to run on lu this complaint of the imperfections
which have be~n pnt upon our organization, and forget to contemplate its beauties
and perfections. Because our Order embraces the silly and the vain, we may not
forget that it also numbers the profoundest thinkers and scholars of the olden time ;
that kings, princes, statesmen, and artists have been its followers; that in our own
country WASHINGTON, FRANJU.IN, and LA FAYll.'TTE did not di~dain to olothe, them·
selves in the simple lambskin emblem of our Ot·der. All we ne ed say of the ha.ute
grades of Masonry, is expressed in the remark attributed to Frederick the Great,
that they were "idle, valueless, and playwork. 11 Ancient Craft Masonry, begin·
nlng with the Entered Apprentice and ending with tbe Royal Arch degree, is a
beantiful, complete, and simple system-founde•J in reason and sense- teaching
the sublimest truths of life and Immortality, the practical duties of everyday oxlstence, and the duties which man owes to God, his neighbor, his country, snd
himself-inculcating a belief in the existence of a Supreme Being, in the immortality of the soul, that all men are equal, that the passions are to he subdued,
and that the moral virtues are to be cultivated with care and practiced with dili- ·
gence. It teaches love and charity to our fellow-man-truth, sobriety, and industry.
The good Mason is a good man. If he fails in the domestic relation of husband or
parent, if he is a bad son or citizen, if he fails to practice Industry, temperance, and
frugality, if he commits fraud or crime,.....in a 1Vord, if he fails in any of the obligations which he owes to his fellow-man, he is a bad Mason.

Masonry !11t)!rfer11 with no Hot, seeks to interpose no restrictions upon reiigio11e
belief, int~rferea wltl1 uo man'• faith. It is in some sort a religion to itself. Holding
firmly to cert11l11 great oardh111l articles of belief, it is never diverted from their
assertion by any 111urc dogma. It deBpises the me're forms of worship; it eschews,
the mere ouremonlal of belief; It permits no new revelations or innovations. It doee
not believe In any earthly power 11s God's vicegerent, or that any man is clothed with
the right to ab1nlve olll!nae•, or 11 himself immaculate or incapable of sin. While it
ha1 ne1·er laid tile weight of It• linger upon any man's conscience, or laid a straw in
the way of tho prugre11 of any church, or sect, or organization, it has confronted
eooieslastlcal power and tyranny In all ages of the world. It has stood up against
the Roman hiP.rarohy In the exerol1e of its arrogant pretensions ; it has defied the
Inquisition with all Its terror•; It bu withstoood priestly nrrogance wherever and
whenever it b aM been a11erted ; and, If tl1e time should ever come in this American
Republic when any church orranlzatlon Rhould deem itself powerful enough to dare
the nttempt to subvert the right• of the people or inte\fere with the liberty <•f con~•.
science, then will that church find an order , in its secrecy, its power, its numbers, •
and its wealth, ready to cope with It to tho bitter, if needs be, the bloody end, in ·
assertion of the rights of man.
Masonry is the friend of education. It enoourages the spread of intelligence , and,
in the long a.go time when the world was In lntelleotulll darkness, .the lights fr om
its altars shed a bright radiance through the surrounding gloom.
The mission of Masonry is not political. It does not seek to Interfere with gov·
ernmental alf.iirs. In past ages it has been charged that in its secret councils plots
have been hatched against authority; but this assertion, though of~en made, has been
as often disproved. It has perhaps occasioually been attempted to be thus used,
as in Mexico , to cover party movements and partisan designs; perhaps, also, when in
New York a :.olitical p&rty was arrayed against it. The royal family of England, both
of the house of Stuart and of Guelph, have been its members; and in more than one
instance the gavel of the Master and the scepter of the King have been wielded by the
same hand. The King of Prussia was once the Master of a Lodl(e. In other conntries
it has been opposed as dangerous with all the power of the State. The teaching of
Masonry is obedience to the law, respect to the government; and while it doe s not in·
terfere in mere party matters, it bears in mind the national honor and is ever earnest
for the nation's good. It was an unhappy thing for the American people that even the
ties of Masonry and the brotherly love of its members were not atl'ong enou17.h to have
spared our land the desolating war of our late civil strife. But, while it was too
feeble to stay fratricidal hands, and powerless to allay sectional and party feeling,
yet, the moment the war began, and all along the time of its bloody progress,
Masonry stretched out its arm to relieve the horrors of the strife. How often on
battle-lie Id has the uplifted hand been stayed by the Masonic sign! How often has
the wounded soldier, bleeding, near to death, felt the grip, strong as the lion's paw,
that has raised him up to life! How often has the Masonic recognition passed in pris·
on and hospital, to the relief of the distressed brother-all the mad passions of the
strife forgotten, all the hatred of the hour smothered down at the signal of a broth·
er's peril! The war, thank God, has ended, and one pa.rt of the Masonic work is
to bury the animosities of the past and to restore throughout our land fraternal love
and brotherly kindness.
'

do we conceive it of practical importance; and yet, to the student of Masonic history,
the research presents a field of interesting and curious speculation. Masonic writers ·
have, many of thorn, groped so far back into the past as to have seemingly Jost them· ·
selves. Some have not hesitated to claim Masonry as coeval with the birth pf man, and .
that Adam was the first Grand Master. Enoch and Tubal Cain a.re made to figure in ·
the legends of the Order. The Eleusinian mysteries, which fiouriMhed in Egypt, a.re to
