Masnnry Is not doln; the half Its duty in California. It needs a reformationsome Martin Luther to preaob against its abuses-some Peter the Hermit to stir its
enthuslasm-- aumu now c1•uaader to awaken it to duty-some inspiration to breathe
into Its carcau anew the brutb of life and give vitality to its dry bones. We are
here a~ aentlnel1 on the outpo1t of oivilization, pioneers in a new land, confronting
tlte mllllona of Aida and looking back to the millions of Europe-a connecting link
between two peopl111 of dltf~rent religions and diverse civilizations. We have many
thlnga to do In our own mld1t. Other orders, less opulent than ours, have journals,
banks of depoalt, and active charities. Church congregations build their edifices
and have t~el~ 1ohool1 and &11oclatlons for social and intellectual pleasures. An organization, hoatlle to ua, and ouu that Is ever acquiring power for its abuse, is planting Its foundations bro11d anll deep-acquiring lands and wealth measured by millions-eteallng, so far aa 11n aa1u1peoting and too indifferent public will permit it, the
education of our children· anll Insinuating itself into all departments· of our Government with untiring and 1leeple11 energy.
It cannot be said that Ha1onry h111 nothing to do-that it has accomplished its
object. It has n thousand thing• to engage Its attention-wants to relieve, worthless brethren to redeem or punbb, temples to build, Intelligence to diBBeminate. Its
Lodge meetings should be made mu re attractive. Sau Francisco should have a representative Lodge, where something should be done beyond the mere work of initiation;
a Lodge to which all Masons may be admissible and where the good of the Order may
be discussed; where visitors may be received and intelligent minds may find intelligent
employment in laying out the work of the Order. This Lodge should be the head
and brain, and the other Lodges the active limbs and members. The Grand Lodge
of the State should be the soul of the whole body, and thus we would have a live,
working, intelligent Institution. It would be a sentinel on the watch tower, ever oq the
lookout fur the enemies of social order, ever vigilant for Its own interests, in which
are involved the interests of society and good government. A National Grand
Lodge should be established, to cement the Order throughout the States into a grand
and harmonious whole; and there should be a Universal Grand Lodgeot' the World,
where representatives of the Lodges of all nations might assemble to consider those
questions affecting alike the interests of' Masonry and the progress and welfare of the
human family. This would be the ,nearest thing to a universal peace "°ogress-a
congress not composed of 9rowned heads, nor governing powers-not a congress
to discuss dynastic questions or territorial bou~arles-not a congress to settle the
clashing authority of' usurped rights-but a convocation of delegates from all nations,
countries, families, colors and interests, embracing the intelligenc.e of the world,
composed of the representative men of .ivery land, consulting for the interests of
the people-not to discuss dogmas nor to prescribe forms of worship-not to regulate vestments nor ceremonials-but to legislate for all God's children, and to see to
the carrying out of their enactments through the moral influence and secret workings of a powerful and universal Order.
Such is my idea ot' a grand and comprehensive Masonry that shall embrace in its
scheme of benevolence the whole family of the brotherhood of man.

Bro. JoHN S. WARD, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented
the following report:1b the M. •. W. •. Grand Lodge of California:-

Your committee, to .whom was referred the resolution offered 1.Jy Bro. RICHARD
DALE, rel11tive to the burial of suicides, have considered the same and respectfully
report that they agree entirely with Past Grand Master BELCHER, in his Annual Ad·
dress in the Communication of 1864, who says :If a Mason forget his duty to God, his fellow, and himself, and commit .suicide,
shall he or may he be buried by his Lodge with Masonic honors ? Several cases
have occurred, a.~ I am informed, in which suicides have been so buried. It should
not alwaJ.s be so. When a Mason has unfortunately been deprived of that reason
which Gou bas given him to enable him· te distinguish between right and wrong,
and, bei~g actualir demented, deprives. himself of life, I see no reason wliy he should
not be mterred with the usual Masomc honors and ceremonials. An insane man
~annot c_ommit ~crime, and it would be an utter forge_tfu~ness of that cha1"ity wyich
is the brightest Jewel of the Craft, to refuse the Masomc rite of burial, when desired
by his rel~tives or friends , to one who had only been unfortunate. Not so, however
with one who willingly, or in consequence of' intemperate habits, destroys !he iif~
which Heaven bas given him for useful and beneficent purposes. We would throw
the mantle of charity over the faults of an erring brother, dead or living, but we
should not lightly overlook bis crimes. By all law, human and divine, he who takes
• his own life i• as guilty as he who takes the life -0f another. B~fore God and man
he is guilty, and it is not fitting that we, as a society, should hold ourselves. out to
the world as the excusers of such crimes.
Entertaining opinions similar to those so well expressed, your committee recorn·
mend that the General Regulation, No. 22, be repealed , and that the following be
adopted in its stead :~
Res~l·oed, That In the case of a suicide of a Master Mason in this jurisdiction, the
Lodge to which he belonged shall determine as to his insanity and as to the propriety
of interring him with Masonic honors.
'
All which is respectfully submitted.
GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, }
JOHN s. WARD,
. Committee.

EDMUND T. WILKINS,

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, from the same committee, presented the
following report : To the M. ·• W." Grand Lodge of California:- .
Your committee, to whom was referred that ·portion of the Grand Master's Ad·
dress in which the attention of the Grand Lodge is directed to the consideration of
the subject of the work and lectures, have given the matter their careful consideration and respectfully report as follows:We fully indorse the views expressed by the Grand Master, which are confirmed
by our association with the representatives of Lodges present at this Communication.
The promulgation of the work does not seem to have been as ·effective under the
present system as it was before the salary attached to the office of Grand Lecturer
was abolished; and the two systems having been fairly tried with the result before
us, we have no doubt of the superiority of the former. It seems to be asking too
much of a brother to expect him to devote as much time as the honest and conscientious discharge of the duties of the position requires, without compensating him, to
a jnst extent, for the value of the time which he is compelled to takjl from his regular
vocation. The position is not a sinecure, but requires, besides intellecW.al capacity,
that peculiar patience of temper and urbanity of manner which distinguishes the
successful instructor of youth. If he accepts the position he must give his time, not

In all these cases the commissioners elected chairmen. This was not in accordance with the provision of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, by which it is provided that "The commissioners * " • shall be presided over by the Master, who

acquaint themselves with Its provisions. If they would do so, the labors of the com- .
mittees of the Grand Lodge would be vastly lessened.

With pride I greet yon on this opening morning ot another yearly festival, with

To Freemasonry the yt!ar has been sufficiently prosperous, as prosperity' is usuall7
estimated. Members have beenadded in sufficient numbers, and the material strength
of the Fraternity, as strength is too often judged, has been in no degree impalrell.
But let ne not deceive ourselves with these appearances. A mere Increase of numben
is no cause of congratulation, and I repeat to you as my solemn conviction, what ha1
been already said by the Grand Masters of perhaps every jurisdiction on this contl·
nent, that if there is one thing which, more than all othlll'B combined, threatens the
downfall of this patriarchal Institution, It is Its growing popularity. A rapid aoccssion
of indllferent members, a too cantious use of the negative ballot, and a cowardl7
indisposition to apply Masonic discipline to those already within the fold- these are
the quicksands and bars on which Freemasonry may yet founder. Through these
faults you are filling yonr ranks with unworthy members, inspired with no loftier
ambition than to live in Indolence upon the toil of their brethren; and following this,
you have been compelled by the very principles of self-preservation to shift your personal obl,gatlons to your brethren, from yourselves Individually, to the Lodge in ita
collective capacity; e.ud then permit the Lodge in turn to 'set up an arbitrary nnd
oll'enslve rule to shut oil' these drones whom your own folly and neglect have
brought into your •household. Thus the Masonic conscience. is comp~lled to
shield itself from th~ Masonic obligation by the specious but shallow pretext tha\
he who appeals for aid has not performed bis duties to the Lodge of which he
is a member. It Is these vices and innovations which may yet destroy the identity of
Masonry. and reduce it lo the level of a mere mutual aid association. I canno\
express to you the chagrin and sorrow I have sometimes experienced in consequence
of these nnhappy conditions. A distressed brother asks for assistance, and he is in
turn asked, as coldly as the banker asks for his securities, If he has paid his du88;
and If bis misfortunes compel him to answer In the negative, no matter what the cause,
or how worthy he may be In other respects, his claims are ignored, and Ire is sen\
empty away. At last be dies, and the penalties of his poverty follow him still. The
last rites, so prized by the appreciative Masou, are denied him, because the Secretar7
has balanced hie account and found him indebted to the Lodge for six month's dues.
A few months later, and the widow of the deceased brother comes in her Jable rob88,

dead Idol was a Mason; and she Is gravely told that her husband died under the ban

These utterance& are distasteful to you, my brethren, but they are well de·
served; and If you would escape from such ammadversions, if you would remove
your noble Institution trom beneath the cloud which overshadows, and beyond
the reach of the tempest which threatens It, begin, as I have suggested, at the very
foundation of the evil. Remember that the strength of the Brotherhood depends
not on the number, but on the character of the members, and let the proper and dill·
gent use or the black ball attest your fidelity to this principle. Be diligent, too, in the
application of discipline. If you find one among you unworthy of conbdence and

Masonic excellence, if may be; but when the conviction Is forced upon you that you

virtue than the mere law of the land Imposes. Let them know that it is not
necessary they should c.ommit some crime for which that Jaw will consign
them to II felon's cell, before they can be punished by the Masonic cooe j but that,
on the contrary, when one Mason acts in bad faith with another in any degree, he haa

received hereafter, come with the full understanding that they are expected to ~ve
rather than receive, to do good to their fellow men rather than be pensioners upon

didate, but assure yourselves, before you accept him, that his temper and metal are

for a series or" years, and not many years will be required.I.. will restore the goodly con·

With these views it has been my constant efl'ort, In visiting Lodges, to Impress upon
my brethren a higher standard of Masonic excellence, more exaotlng tests of fitness
In candidates, a more rigid observance of our solemn personal obligations to each
other in all our Intercourse, and more readiness to punish every departure from those
obligations. I have urged upon them everywhere, that the so-called lesser evUs of
society, of which the law of the land takes no cognizance-intemperance, profanity,
evil speaking, hypocrisy and deception-re all Masonic ofl'ences; and, as we would
preserve the ancient lustre and hallowed charm which has so long encircled the Fra·
ternity, we can not be too zealous in their condemnation and punishment. And I am
happy in the belief that these etforts have not been entirely barren of results, and
only regret that I have net been able to extend my personal observation and efforts
further.
I have visited about thirty of the Lodges, In all of which, but one, I have witnessed

Soon after our last Annual Communication the Master of Norihern Light Lodge
Inquired if It was necessary to take a ballot for the degrees, when the report of the
committee was unfavorable; and ~replied, without much thought or consideration, tJa.t
a ballot In such case was unnecessary ; that on reading the report the Master should
at once declare the candidate rejected, and the Secretary report him accordingly.
Soon thereafter the same question was asked by Pentalpha Lodge, and I then gave
the matter more reflection; and, on consultation with some of my brethren in
whom I had great confidence, I advised the Master of the latter Lodge to take the
ballot In all cases, until a different rule should be promulgated by the Grsnd Lodge.
l>ractlcally, it can make no difference which course is pursued, for It is hardly possi·
ble that an election could take place over an unfllvorable report; but in theory and
principle the questJon Is one of some importance. Taking the ballot Implies the right
to elect as well as the right to reject; and the right to elect does not, In any just
sense of the term, exist in the presence of an unfavorable report. If, indeed, the bal·
lot should be fllvorable under such circumstances, it would undoubtedly be the duty
of ·the Master to regard the unfavorable report, until withdrawn, as a standing objec·
tion to lnltiatJon; and the ballot would thus have been an empty ceremony, without
any possible effect-a folly of which Masonry ought never to be guilty. .Again, It
might well happen that the brethren making the report, were the only ones In the
Lodge having objections to the candidate; and they might necessarily be absent at
the time of the ballot. All the other brethren might desire the election of the candidate, in spite of the unfavorable report, and such election, if thus had, (unless as
suggested above, the unfavorable report be regarded as a standing object.ion, ) might
be followed by imm!ldiate initiation, and thus the absolute right of the objecting mem·
bers be entirely disregarded and overborne. A rule which thus opens the way to the
perpetration of an absolute wrong, cannot be correct in principle.
.
.And again, if the ballot is to be taken, notwithstanding the unfavorable report, it
presents an opportunity and temptation for the exercise of every variety of improper
intluences to secure an election, The report Itself points out the particular brethren
who are dissatisfied, and theywlll be Immediately assailed, b;v those who particular~
~esire an election, with every conceivable argument and persuasion; and thus the
mdependence and sacredness of the ballot be entirely destroyed : .for , hol( often these
personal Influences and the desire to gratJty brethren would affect the result, those
who understand the weakness of human nature can judge as well as I. The very fact
alone that such a course ls likefy to lead to the exercise of these influences, Is a sufficient reason why the ballot should not be taken. The Lodg~ should not be allowed
the opportunity to elect, if it would. I am abundantly satisfied that, upon reason and
principle, for the peace and harmony of Lodges, for the pJJrlty and independence
of the ballot, and for the honor and protection of committees In case of tUir absence ·
from Lodge wh~n their reports are considered, a ballot ought never to be allowed on
an unfavorable finding. There is nothing In our Constitution which requires a ballot
in such a case, nor is there any provision which necessarily rmplies as much; and In
the absence of such provisions I am in full concurrence with Bro. MACKEY, that, by
the Common Law of Masonry, an unfavorable report Is equivalent to a rejection. I
am aware that in several of the other jurisdictions it has been held that the ballot
should be taken In all cases; but an lnvestJgatlon will reveal the fact that these decll·
ions have been simply in obedience to some express by·law, legulatlon, or provi1lon

As I have advised the M11ster of a Lodge, in one instance at least, to pursue the

An unsettled question touching physical qualiflcatiollil was presented for solution
In November last. A candidate had been elected in another jnrlsdiotion, e.nd had
there received the first degree. Subsequently he lost a leg, and after this misfortune
applied for the remalulng degrees here, with the proper certificate and permit fi'.om
the Lodge where initiated. It was claimed that something was due to the fact of his
having received the first degree; that he was already a Mason, and the question was
not one of making, but simply of finishing; the.the had already acquired some rights,
and occupied e. position very different from that of a profane seeking initiation, and
that his advancement would be no violation of the regulation touching physlce.l conformation. Certainly there is some force and good reasoning in all this. It may be
also conceded the.t In this age, and with Masonry e.s now practiced, a purely speculative science, the mental and moral qualifications are fe.r more important the.n the physical; and much of the reasoning on which the ancient requirements were based, he.s
now no application. Besides, the · regulations apply in terms only to the uninitia.ted,
and not to him who has alr06dy commenced his Masonic course. That it would be
competent for this Grand Lodge to relax this rule as to the advancement of c.§n!lidates, I have no doubt; but whether it would be advisable to do ao, you in your wisdom
must determine. On the one hand ;ases arise like the present where the rigid exaction of physical perfection at every stage of the course, seems to operate as a serious
hardship to the individual. He is, in fact and theory, already a Mason, but must remain perpetually, through no fault of his own, shut off from all further light, his Masonic
education unfinished, and himself excluded from the enjeyment of all Lodge prlvi·
leges, e.nd even from Masonic burial. On the other fiand, the conservative feature of
Masonry, its unchangeable character, ls one of its greatest charms, and its chief bulwark and defense ; and the work of change and modification once begun might lead
to most disastrous results. With no positive rule or precedent to guide me, I felt obliged, by the analogies of the case, to pronounce the applicant disqualified for advancement.
I have been repeatedly asked, can a Mason be tried for acts committed before his
initiation t There has been no adjudication on this question in this jurisdiction, and
it has been a matter of much ~harp controversy, and various decisions in other Grand
Lodges. Some he.ve asserted the right brciadly and without any qualification, and
others have denied it i n wto. Neither of these rules are, in my judgment, correct, but should be qualified by certain general principles, by the intelligent
application of which, every conceive.ble case may be properly disposed of. There
are a.eta not wrong or immoral in them8elve1, which are still inhibited by the
Masonic obligation. Buch ~ ad, committed before Initiation, could never "bfl the
subject of investigation; for it is only by virtue of having been done in violation of
the Masonic obligation that it could be an offense at all; 11nd how can one violate an
obligation before he has taken it? But those acts which are in themselves wrong or
immoral, though committed before initiation, may be afterwards punished, unleai thP
Lodge, at the time of election, had knowledge of the facts. But if the Lodge, with a
full knowledge of the fact that the candidate had perpetrated a wrong deaerving disci.
pline, should still elect him, such election should be considered a condonation of the
offence; and good ·faith would preclude any further investigation. In such case· the
Lodge itself should .be punished, for electing knowingly a... on.worthy applicant.
I decided the question in accordance with these views, and as it is a matter of some
practical Importance, I hope the Grand Lodge will.approve or disapprov.e the decision.

Representatives of this Grand Lodge abroad have been nominated by me in two
Instances only : Past Grand Master STEPHENS, of Florida, near the Grand Lodge
of tllat State, and '.Past Grand Master :M:cCRAKEN, of Oregon,- near the Grand Lodge
of Oregon. These appointments have been made as responses, rather than
otherwise, to like appointments within our jurisdiction by the Grand Lodges named.
I do not refer to this as indicating on my part any distrust of the propriety of making
such appointments. On the contrary, I am fully persuaded that a general interchange of representatives, among all the jurisdictions, might be made productive of
great good, by its tendency, if the office should be aotively exercised, to draw us
nearer together and make us better acquainted by the exohange of such fraternal
conrtesied and hospitalities, and to consolidate the whole brotherhood of the continent in a single and more homogeneons family. But to produce any such results,
these Representlltives must manifest themselves In some other manner than by the
mere formal presentation of their credentials and exhibition of their jewels. While I
entertain these opinions, yet, as the system of Grand Lodge Representatives is now
managed-the position being, in practice, an office without a fnnotlon-a name without substance or significance-I have elected to make such appointments only when
tlle corresponding Grand Lodge has first accredited a Representative to us.
Since our last Communication, about forty of our Lodges have adopted amendments to their by-laws abolishing or reducing the affiliation fee, in accordance with
the recommendation of the Grand Lodge. In probably two-thirds of these cases we
have been obliged to return the certificates for want of form and sufficiency. This
has imposed considerable labor on tlle Grand Master and Grand Secretary, and the
same process is likely to be continued, unless the Grand Lodge shall take further
action in the matter. Now; If it was right and proper for the Grand Lodge to recommend these amendments (and I think it was), it seems to me it would be equally right
and proper for the Grand Lodge to enact the amendment, and not leave the matter
half done , for eaeh: 1me of the hundred and seventy Lodges to complete. I accordingly most earnestly renew the recommendation ·of my immediate predecessor, that
the Grand Lodge do now abolish, in toto, the aftlliation i'ee.

I also most cordlaliy renew another recommendation of my predecessor, that the
rule of one baliot for the three degrees be made obligatory on all the Lodges. Unless
this Is done, some of our Lodges will soon be again bur7lened with long lists of unfinished Masons. Besides, atler a person has been Initiated; I do not think he should be
then left In a situation where the caprice or ill-will of a single member can absolutely
and without any just cause stop his Masonic course. He has the!\ some rights as a
Mason, and should be permitted to advance, unless there be some assignable cause
for stopping him.

lam also convinced that the Grand Lodge made 11 serious mistake when it abolished

I can not close this address without the expression of my warmest gratitude for the
uniform kindness, conrtesy, and hospitality with which I have been everywhere re·
ceived and welcomed by my Masonic brethren. My official visits have been to me sea·
sons of great personal pleasnre and enjoyment, as well as Masonic labor and profit, and

To the Grand Lecturer I am muc.h indebted for his prompt and efficient eervloH,
whenever such service could be available; and to the Grand Secretary my thanka
are due' in a special degree, for his constant and uniform willingness to give me hie
time, his labor, and his Masonic knowledge, to aid me in the discharge of all the
duties of my office.
And here, my brethren, I complete the record of my official acts. I am painfully
aware that this paper has grown to most inordinate length. But, recognizing to the
fullest extent my responsibility to yon, I desired to so present my every act that you
might both see what had.been done, and the mainspring and motives of doing it. I
invite your careful scrutiny, hopeful, indeed, that I may receive your approbation,
but certain that you will not cenenre me unjustly. And so, with many thanks for the
honors you have already conferred on me, and with the earnest wish that all along
the great future, wherever your fortunes may be cast, peace, prosperity, and the
golden fi·uite of faithful service may cluster around and attend you, I cheerfully
submit my work to your inspection, and myself to your further will and pleasure.

Since the last .Annual Comm.unioation only eight special dispensations have been
ordered by the Grand Master to be issued from this office. Of these, three were to
authorize reballots upon petitions of rejected applicants for the degrees, within the
period of prohibition prescribed by the general provisions of our laws; three were
to permit the election of officers at times other than the regular one named in the
Constitution; and two were to allow ballots to be had upon petitions for degrees
without the custome.ry reference to committees of Investigation. The petitions for
the issue of these dispensations were all ordered to be submitted to the Grand Master
by the unanimous ballots of the Lodges whence they came, in the manner prescribed
by our laws; they 1111 presented reasons apparently sufficient to justify his favorable
consideration; and they, with such other papers as relate to them, are herewith submitted .
Several letters, circulars, and pamphlets, relative to an" unpleasantness" within
the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Canada, cauHed by a declaration of independence on the part of certain Lodges owing allegiance thereto, and the consequent
formation ot' the soi-disant " Grand Lodge of Quebec," have been received by the
undersigned during the past year. As comment or expression of opinion thereupon
would perhaps not find proper place in a paper such as this, they are submitted to
the Grand Lodge without either.
The interchange of Representatives between the various Grand Lodges of the
world, but more especially those of North America, has of late years attained a very
prominent consideration; and, though it may be doubtful whether much practical
usefulness has resulted, or will result, from such appointments among the American
Grand Lodges, whose present system of reports by Committees of Correspondence
furnishes infinitely more information each to the other than any Representative would
ever be likely to collect and transmit, yet the custom affords a happy channel for the
exchange of one of those pleasant courtesies, the exercise of all which tends to bring
into closer and more intimate relations the several M..sonic Senates of the Union,
and, through them, to increase still further the strength of the bonds which so happily unite together all the individuals of the great Fraternity. Readily influenced by
this feeling, the Grand Lodge of California has, with glad alacrity, accredited Representatives trom and appointed them to a number of the other Grand Lodges of America, and; It Is perhaps needless to say, will always be ready to extend or reciprocate
such courtefl)es In the future.
N"o collectecj list of the appointments made to or by this Grand Lodge has heretofore beeu presented, and, as their number has grown, within the past few year8 , to
tolerably respectable proportlona, it has been thought not unadvieable to record
here that little additional portion of our history. A careful examination of our
recordd shows the follo.wlng :In 1857, Grand Master W1LLIAX H. HOWARD announced the appointment of the

Of proposed amendments to the by-laws of chartered Lodges, sixty-one have been
filed in this office since the last A.nnunl Communication, the largest portion of the111
being the consequence of the recommendation of the Grand Lodge at that time, rt!a·
tive to the fee for affiliation. Of the number named , twenty propose a reduct.ion of
that fee to one dollar; fifteen propose its entire abolition ; ten propose to r educe, and
three to increase, the quarterly dues; two propose to decrease, and two to increase,
the fees for the degrees; seven propose changes in the times of meeting; and two
·propose a separa.te ballot for each degree. Action in the Lodges upon all these hav·
ing been in accordance with the law, they have received the te.m porary approval of
the Grand Master; and, as required by the Constitution, they are now presented to
the Grand Lodge l'or final action, as are also copies of the proposed by-laws of the
seven Lodges existing under dispensation.

ALABAMA.
The forty·ninlh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the State of
Alabama was held in Montgomery, commencing December 6, 1869-the M.-. W.'.
GEORGE D. NORRIS, Grand.Master;preeiding, and the R.'. W.·. DANIEL SAYRE being
Grand Secretary. Representatives were present from two hundred and twenty-four
chartered Lodges.
Past Gre.nd Master HA.7.&LRIOG, of Indiana, being in the city of Montgomery, w11s
waited upon by a committee of the Grand Lodge, introduced, received with all the
honors, and placed upon the right of the Grand Master.
The Addrees of the Grand Master is rather long to suit our ideas, too much
apace being devoted to the discussion of abstract questions. Ali this -will do, if the
ventilation of rhetoric be all that is advisable. But we confess to a liking for b;evity,
and the discussion of practical matters in these" Messa.gee from the Governor."
The address is well written, however, and is e.n able document. Due and feeling
notice is taken of death's doings in the removal of Bro. SAMUEL H. DIXON, Past
Senior Grand Warden, and of Bro. THOMAS McDOUGAL, for e. long time Grand
Tyler of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master alludes to and approves the action of the Grand I,odge of
Louisiana in relation to the Grand Orient of France. His remarks are severe but
just. We believe there has been perfect unanimity among all the American Grand
Lodges on this subject, and it is right that it should be so. Some see and pursue
that inevite.ble African who is "hid~en in this fence," with more zeal than do
others ; but all agree that tho action of the. Grand Orient was a Masonic outrage
upon the prerogatives of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, and all stand by this last
in its defense of its rights, and•in putting their ban upon the intruder.•
The earnest attention of the Grand Lodge Is called to the necessity of establish·
Ing a" Masonic Orphan's Home," to be conducted under the auspices of the Grand
Lodge. Returns had been received from seventy.five Lodges only, and yet they re·
ported five hundred and flfty-onfl orphans. On such. a fact how powerful is the
~
following appeai of the Grand Master:What a number, whose wail comes to as pleading for help. Sha\1 we give it to
them 1 Will we not take these desolate ones, left to us by onr brothers, and· clothe,
feed , and educate them for deeds of usefulness? Let us engage In this noble, Godlike work, and leave for our posterity a monument more lasting than brass, and to
our Order the proud consciousness of practically exemplifying those three great
Masonic 11rinciples, Faith, Hope, and Charity. Then indeed can we see, like Jacob
In his vision, the starry-decked heaven with Its glittering jewels set in the vast concave, innumerable und unlimited, and the ladder reaching to its heights, with angels
ascending and .descending, the flutter of whose wings deliciously waves in succes1lve billows, balmy air, fresh from the throno "of God.
The Grand Master reprobates the usage of granting "dimits to every brothe~
who may'.' take a mift'" at ·the proceedings of hie Louge, ~at the conduct of a
brother. He denies the doctrine that 'a brother has an.absolute right to a dimit, though
he be equl\re upon the books, and thinks, as we do, that the Lodge has something to
aay on that point as well as upon the first e.dmission. He recommends-and the

The report of the Grand Secretary 11 brief, but it contains this little gein, of a
Mason's good will and llvlng charity, which we cull for the benefit of our own
readers:In January. last I received a letter from one who si~ns himself-" Fraternally, F.

The receipts of the Grand Lodge for the year had been $8,967 11, and the expen·
ditures $4,204 95.
The Report of tho Committee on Correspondence is again from the pen of that
worthy and veteran Masonic Scribe, Bro. WILLIAM C. PKNIOK. What he writ~s is ·
.always good reading, whether one coincides with the author in sentiment or not.
In this report, filling almost one hundred pages of the journal, we have a learned,
full, and interesting review of the proceedings of forty-seven Grand Lodges, our own
. for 1868 being among the number. Upon 11 suggestion of the Grand Master of Ohio,
that • subordinate Lodges be permitted to confer on all who have been active mem·
bers of some :Lodge in that jurisdiction for a period of twenty·oue years, the title of
Emeritus members, relieving them dnring life from the payment of dues and assess·
ments, and continuing them in the enjoyment of all Lodge prMleges," Bro. PENIOK
..makes these remarks, which are very much like telling one's experience In" class
meeting":Well, we think thM this will not do. Twenty·olie years will not suffice. We, our·
self, was made a Mason in 1826. Since 1847, we have been more active, have done
more in and for Masonry than before, and in the second twenty-one years in Ma·
sonry, we have been enabled to do more than in all our life before. No Mason should
be relieved of these duties while he is able to perform them. But when age and
physical disability come on us, our property forcibly taken from us, our helpless
families dependent on us, this privilege proposed by Grand Master MATTHEWS might
be well enough for old and worn out Masons-those sixty-live or seventy years of
age-who have been regular paying members for a long time. But there are man;}'
Masons, who have been such twenty-one years, who are in the prime of hfe and
have much moneys and means, and who are both able and willing to work and con·
tribute to the relief and benefit of the needy brethren and the general cause.
Bro. PENICK has a genial and somewhat extended notice of our Californi!' pro•
ceedings for 1868. He speaks in commendation of the Addresa of Grand Master
DAVIES, and has a kind, and, we fear, too partial notice of on~ first effon in this·
line of writing the Correspondence Committee's Report. When we see our illustrl·
ous predecessor, Bro. RHEES, we will certainly give him Bro. PKNIOK's message,

We ·have also received a pamphlet entitled" Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of
Ancient, Free and Aooepted Masons of Canada, at a Speoial Emergent Communlca·
tion, held in Montreal, December 1, 1869 ;" and still another, with this title:
" Statement concerning the Grand Lodge of Ancient, Free and Aocepted Masons of
Quebec." As both pamphiete refer to the same subject, we will consider them
together; and in this connection, as there is trouble In the camp· over the border,
other than that caused by the Fenian Invasion, we have tried our best to get at the
kernel of the nut lnclosed in the very rough covering of the statements on both
sides. Having onlled to our aid the very excellent Masonic spectacles of Bro.
DRUMMOND, of Maine, who is too clear-headed and warm-hearted to make intentional
or grave mistakes, we think we c11n see about where the land lies. One thing we
must say at the outset: we do not like the temper displayed in either of these
pamphlets. Both writers Rnd parties seem to us to go too much upon the "you are
another" style, to help outsiders to see clearly where the blame or the right of the
matter is. If we fail to give our readers a clear insight into the merits of this rather
ugly controversy, the parties thereto must bear their full share of the blame. We
shall make no intentional mistake, for we can very well see that much can be plausibly said on both sides.
Briefly, we believe the matter to stand Rome what thus : The Grand Lodge of
Canada claims jurlsdlotion over all that is at present included within what icas
Upper and Lower Canada-now.the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and that no
other Grand Lodge can be Instituted therein without its permission. The Province
of Quebec being a part of such general jurisdiction, the ground, it is claimed, is and
has been Masonlcally occupied. The brethren in Quebec, on the contrary, who have·
established a new Grand Lodge and ask us and all other Grand Lodges to extend to
them the right .hand of full recognition and fellowship, claim that each department
or separate province of the now Dominion of Canada Is as distinct a political
organization as Is each State in our Federal Union. Hence the claim Is that the
brethren of Quebec have as much right to a Grand Lodge RB had the Mnsons of
Mnlne, or· Oregon, or any other of the Commonwealths of the Union; and that, if
they were nominally attached to and a part of the Grand Lodge of Canada, that
fact does not deprive them of their rights, and they point to the Grand Lodges of
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as folr and legitimate precedents.
The Grand Lodge of Canada denies both premises and conclusions; masonicaJlf
expel the offending Masons; read their Lodges out of the " Masonic Church;" and 1
appeal.to all the world beside to treat the Quebec Grand Lodge and Masone 11.11
clandestine, and to put them under the ban of non-Intercourse.
Stripped of a mass of verbiage and irrelevant ml\tter, we believe this to be a
fair statement of the real poiut at Issue. For whether Grand Master STEVEl!IBO did
or did not sell himself to the enemy and desert his old friends, or whethe~ certain
Masons did or did not tell the " truth. the whole truth, and nothing but the troth "
about certain interviews that were had or asked for, Is, in our estimat!0.1 111lde

We find the questions involved in this matter so thoroughly and ably discussed by
the Grand Master and the Chairman of the Committee of Correspondence, (Bro.
DRUHl!OND), of Maine, that we feel we cannot do better than give an epitome of the
reasonings of the latter. Of course Canada denies the right of the Quebec brethren
to form this new Grand Lodge w'ithout her consent, no matter whether a major·
ity of the Lodges In that Province did or did not p11.rticipate in the action.
Prior to 1867, the to. rit'>ry over which the Grand Lodge of Canada claims jurisdiction constituted but one Province, caned the "Province of Conada," with bnt
one Legislature •. lo 1867, however, there was a separation into two Provinces~me
called .the "Province of Quebec," and the other the "Province of Ontario." But
these tw.o, with those of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and we think, Prince
Edward's Island, also, were joined in a federate Union to be called" The Dominion
of Canada.'' Ever since, politically, it cannot be denied that the "Province of
Que bee " is as distinct a government as the "Province of Nova Scotia," or the State
of California. Each Provinc.o has its Legislature, and the whole Dominion its gen·
era\ Parliament. The main question then, as Bro. DRUMMOND clearly puts it, is this :When a portion of the territory, in which a Grand Lodge has exclusive jurisdic·
tion. Is erected by the civil government into an Independent State or Province, do
the Lodges therein pos•ess the l"ight to form an independent Grand Lodge? This
question was, until comparatively recently, considered to be settled. It was univer·
sally conceded thl\t the Lodges do have such right. But unfortunately the question
arose lately in such manner as to be connected with a political question, and of

course it did not receive that calm and dispassionate consideration in some quarters
which;Mnsonic questions should receive; and the law which had been well settled,
w11s questioned. We propose, therefore, to refer to soDl.e of the precedents and the
law as established hy the fathers, which some of their sons wonld now annnl.
The precedents cited by our brother of Maine, and which seem to justify the
action of the Quebec brethren, are these :-Virginia and West Virginia, quite
recently; New Hampshire and Massachusetts in 1789; Maryland and Virginia, '.n
connection with the District of Columbia, in 1810; Maine and Massachusetts 1ll
1820; Iowa and Minn8'Jota in 1847; Idaho and Washington in 1868. In an these
(except the ftr•t named) the ground contended for by the Quebec Grand Lodge
seems to have been conceded. The first real dispute arose in 1867, when the Grand
Lodge of West Virginia was formed, aud it is wen known that politics rather than
Masonry started and controlled that discussion. Even the Granb Lodge of Canada
was formed without the consent of the parent Grand Lodge, and so were the Grand
Lodges of Nova Scotia and New l,l!'unswick, both of which were recognized immediately by the Gl'and Lodge of Canada. Of the thirty-nine Lodges in the Province
of Quebec, twenty-one were represented. One, however; afterwards withdrew, still
leaving twenty, a majority of the whole; 11nd all the proceedings seem to have
bee.n orderly and Masonic. In view, then, of all the facts of the case, we .are rather
disposed to assent to the regularity of the formation of the " Grand Lodge of
Quebec."
We submit these facts and opinions to our brethren of the Grand Lodge without any recommendation as to formal action. If, however, any is desirable, we

Bro. PAWKINS says be does not understand the California institution called" Trial

ence taught ~s was little better than a broad farce, each Lodge, when charges are
brought, Is to elect a Commission of. Master Masons, not less than seven nor more
than nine in number, over which. the Master is to preside and decide questions of
Masonlo law that may arise. This Commission hears al! the testimony and arguments_, and renders the verdict, and also fixes the punishment, if found guilty; a
majority of the whole number determining the result. Thie is report~d by the
Master to the Lodge, and a record made, which is all the Lodge bas to do with the
matter. An appeal, of course, lies to the Grand Lodge. Thie le our California institution of "Trial Commissioners," and practically It has worked so well that we
recommend our Florida brethren to adopt the same method.

The great central truth-the alpha of Masonr:v-fs that God lives and iroverns the
world, e.t once the Supreme Architect and the Universal Father; that all mankind
are His children, the objects of His love, e.nd entitled to our consideration as mem·
bers of the so.me great family. What wonder, then, that in the long weary centu·
ries through which man has struggled on towards the iroal of a common equality, an
Institution of which this is the central idea should command the devotion of thoso
who saw, even dimly, the logice.l sequence of this grand conception of the brotherhood of mankind. No human institution inculcates this truth with surh force e.s
Masonry. It views m1tn separated from his accidents. It looks through the trappings
of wealth, the insigni1t of rank, the humble garb of honest poverty" and sees alik~
beneath them e.11-the MAN. Within its charmed circle all are equal. Whether com·
Ing from the hovel of the peasant or the palace of the prince ; at Its portals t_hey
leave all worldly distinctions, e.nd meet on the level of its checquered fioor, brothers
e.nd equals by virtue of their manhood. The humblest and the proudest must travel
the same paths to attain Me.sonic knowledge; are bound to the fraternity and each
other by the so.me sacred ties ; their equal covenants are made in the presence of
the same Almighty Father. To you, my brethren, these statements are but truisms.
But if the uninitiated would ponder them with a sincere desire to discover the
springs of that Dower by which Masonr,r bolds the life-long allegiance of so many
men, they wonld go far in assisting him to e. just conclusion. From this perfect
equality of a.II Me.sons, he will see how we naturally deduce those duties which we
owe to our fellow-men; a.II summed up in the injunction : "Do unto others e.s yon
would that they should do unto you."

The subtle, indefinable influence, the quick, 1tpprehensive sympathy, engendered
by the possession of e. common secret held sacred and inviole.ble, can never be fully
comprehended by those who have not themselves felt its mystic power. It quiCkens
the impulses of charity, sharpens the sense of integrity, softens the asperities of
political warfare, tones down the dogmatic acrimony of theological discussion, mitigates the horrors of war, and prompts to deeds of truest chivalry-of irenerous self. sacrifice. Many a tombstone, standing where pestilence has blazed its desolating
way through crowded cities, is but e. monumental record of the self-sacrificing spirit
thus developed. A striking illustration of its infiuence came under my own observe.·
tion a few yea.rs since. In a rural district, where the very name of the disease la ·
terror, e. Mason fell sick with small-pox. He was deserted by all eave one young
me.n, bound to him only by the Me.sonic tie, who watched pver him while living, and
alone cast the evergreen into his early grave. A few days later this young man
came to the city suffering with the initial fever of the disease, and asked me to take
him to the pest-house, to remain until the danger of lofectinir bis friends was past.
In answer to my questions he tohl me how he had contracted the disease, remarkinir
that "the man we.s a Me.son, and he couldn't see him lie there and suffer without
care." He me.de no ado about it, and seemed unconscious that )le had performed an
act of self-sacrificing devotion requiring the highest type of courage. This young
me.n's surroundings, the atmosphere of his daily life, had not been of au elev1tting
character. More than likely he neglected the "mint, anlso., and cummin" of the
law, e.nd might have been termed e. reprobate by those who adhere rather to the
letter which killeth, than to the spirit which giveth life ; but this compellinir power
of Masonry he.d taken root in his heart e.nd blossomed into deeds redolent of the
sweet odors of charity, and blessed in the sight of Heaven. The infiuence of this
spirit-I might almost say this instinct of brotherhood-in ·mitigating the horrors of
we.r, is attested by many well-known instances, and many more are known only to
those who were parties to them. It snatched Putnam from the torturing hands ef
his captors in the old French war. It more than onCP. mmerved the arm of Butler,
when, with Brandt and his savage followers, he swept with fire an<l sword the lovely
valley of the Wyoming. In the le.st great struggle for national existence it ministered
to the necessities of our brave defenders, who languished in Southern prisons,

Ablltract of .Decisions.
1. An applicant for the honors of Ma•onry petitions for memhershfp as well as
for the degrees, and when raised to the third degree, he Is a member of the Lodge
which elected'him. Signing the By.Laws is an important act of lrlentity, but is not
indispensable to membership.
2. It is unmasonic to ridicule any or all of the three great lights in Masonry, and
a Freemason guilty of such .in offense is unfit to be installed Master of a Lodp;A.
3. EveTy candidate, before ioitie.tion, must solemnly avow a belief in God ; a
subsequent sincere. avowal of a disbelief in God is a practical renunciation of .l!'ree·
masonry.
4. Dl~bellef In the divinity of J esos Christ does not, in any sense, affect Masonic
standing.

expulsion.
.

orets of the chair.

delay, when neceesary to a dispassionate examination.
8. Persons under sentence of suspen&ion for non.payment of dUAR, by an extinct
or dormant Lodge, can be restored only by the Grand Lodge, upon the payment of
all arrearages to the Grand Secretary.
9. No brother can be lawfully elected and installed Worshipful Master without
previous service as Master or Warden, except by dispensation.
10. An objection to the advancement of a candidate, made in open Lodge, or to
the Worshipful Master, most be respected nntil removed or waived.
11. If the Master elect declines installation, the old M.ister holds over, unless a
dispensation be obtained, by common consent, to elect another.
12. In trials, where the accused can not be served with notice, the record should
set forth that his residence is unknown.
13. Entered Apprentices who, by their own neglect, have fail~d to apply for ad·
vancement within one year after tllilir initiation, must petition and be recommended
anew for the second and third degrees, and pass through all the forms of refurence,
report, and ballot. The same rule applies to Fellow Crafts.
.

member, or in the oldest Lodge in the jnrisdictlon of which he resfdea.

16. Objection to the advancement of a candidate before or after election, with·
out reasons, in either degree, Is a permanent objection until the objection Is removed or waived ; and until then, the Lodge can not advance the candidate, nor
give consent to any other Lodge to entertain his application.
17. Aller the lapse of a reasonable time for objections to be waived or with·
drawn, notice of rejection should be given as In other cases, and the money 11coom·
panying the petition should be returned.
18. Ballotings take place at regular meetings only, except in cases of dlspensa·
tion or trials. Examinations as to proftolency may be had in open Lodge at any
·
time before or after balloting.
19. Every candidate for initiation most have the limbs, members, and senses that
a man ought to have. The fixed and unohanireable landmarks of Masonry regard
neither the manner, time, place, or cause of di~memberment, disHguremont, motila·
tion, or di~ability. The fact, alone , like the law, is to govern a Mason.

In this jurisdiction the work usually devolved upon Committees of Correspondence
is thrown upon the Grand Master. Two years since, Grand Master HAZELRIGG made
quite a labored argument to show that, this was not only proper, but by far t.he be Rt

that some of the then Grand Master's successors would differ from him in opinion•
Our prophecy has proveo true. Grand Master R10E acknowledges the receipt of the
proceedings of forty-three Grand Lodges, and adds to the announcement these wellconsidered suggestions, which the' Grand Lodge of Indiana would do well to heed
and follow :·
Having had but little time to devote to an examination of these proceedings, I am
not able to present to you an extended review of Masonry in other jurisdictions, or
of the busineas transacted by other Grand Lodges. I regret that this is the case, for
I tlllnk that a full report should be presented at each Annual Communication. In
every State but ours· this labor i~ performed by a Committee appointed for that purpose, who presdnt at each annual meeting a summary of the busmeas and work of all
the other jurisdictions. These reports are printed with the proceedings of the Grand
Lodges, and thus furnish to the Craft a knowledge of the working of Masonry abroad,
as well as at homo. There can be no good reason why we should stand as a single
· exception to a prnctlce that has so long and so universally prevailed. There seems
to me to be a selfishness, a coldness, and an almost want of courtesy in this exclusiveness. Ours is one of the largest Grand Lodges In this country, and we like to be
remember~d as members of the great Masonic family. Let as cultivate the social

Abstract of Decisions.
1. A Lodge has clearly the right to delegate authority to nny other Lodge, to
confer the Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees on a candidate who hes received
the first or Entered Apprentice degree in it. A majority vote is all that Is required
to grant such authority •
2. A candidate wbo has received the Entered Apprentice degree in a Lodge in a
neighboring jurisdiction, and 11pplies to a Lodge In this jurisdiction for the Fellow
Oraft and Master Mason degrees, must apply the same as a profane for initiation, and
a unanimous ballot must be had before the ea.id degrees can be conferred.
8. One ballot only is required for the election of a candidate for the three degrees
of Ancient Craft Masonry.
4. Charges can be preferred against an Entered Apprentice for nnmasonlc con·
duct, and it' fonnd guilty, the Lodge can expel, suspend, or reprimand him.
6. Brother A, B. having received a majority of all the votes cast for Senior
Warden of a Lodge, was du ly elected, and should hnve been installed, unless a good
and sufficient reason be shown why he should not. The fact of his being suspected
ot' voting for himself is not a sufficient reason to bar him from being installed as Senior
Warden.
6. A candidate who has received the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
degrees in a Lodge In a neighboring jurisdiction , and moving into this State and
applying for the Master Mason's degree, must ftrst obtain the consent of the Lodge
In which he received t he two first degr ees, and then pass through the orceal of a
unanimous ballot before he can lawfully receive the Master Mason degree.
7. When a brother has been tried autl found guilty of a Masonic offense, and th
penalty has been ftxed by the Lodge, notice of his intention to appeal does not
operate as a bar to the proceedings. The Worshipful Master should carry out the
order of the Lodge by Inflicting the penalty.
8: A brother Master Maso.n in good and regular standing , dues all paid to date,
is entitled to a dimit when demanded by himself in person or by petition.
9. An expelled Mason is what we masonically term dead; and his reHtoration In
the Order Is therefore equivalent to the admission of a profane for the my~teries of
Masonry. In addition to the usual petition, be must afso petition t he Lodge from
which he was expelled, for admission.
10. W,hen ch..rges are preferred against a brother for unmasonic conduct, In due
form , and in accordance with the Constitutlou of this State governing trials, etc,,
the Lodge can not refuse to entertain said charges.
Jll. A Lodge can not reconsider a vote on the petition of an applicant for either
the mysteries of Masonry or for aftlliatlon, when duly rejected.
12. A candidate for the mysterie9 of Masonry must be without blemish and have
the full and perfect use of his limbs.

From our brethren in evel'y quarter of the globe come messages of approval of the
course taken by our Grand Lodge, and fo no instance, where tile matter of dillerence
has been clearly understood, has Louisiana been condemned for the tirm stand she
ha< taken. Even the Supreme Council of England, of the Scottish Rite, has adopted
resolutions censuring the Grand Orient of 1''rance for having accorded recognition to
a spurious body of men, who indeed claim to be Masons, but who have never been
elsewhert1 recognized as such, and who have no legal or proper right to the title,
npon so specious and so false a plea as that given by Grand Muster MELLIN.&:T, and
for its improper infringement of the jurisdict.ional rights of our Grand Lodge.
It seems to me hardly possible that a body, so respectable and intelligent as the
Grand Orient of France is acknowledged to be, can much longer persist in this great
wrong to Masonry, and to our Grand Lodge. From indications lately made known
to me by a distinguished brother now in Europe, who has taken a great interest in
this question and in our welfare, I have reason for believing that the hasty action of

The Report of the Committee· on Correspondence is from the pen of Bro. JAMES
B. ScoT, a. veteran in this service, who wields the pen of a ready writer, and always ..
gives us a document well worth the reading. The report before us is a review of the' '
proceedings uf forty-four American Grand Lodges and of fifteen in fore ign countries,
filling up some 14.5 pages of the pamphlet: Oar brother, in his review of the pro·
ceediogs of California for 1868, pays a merited compliment to the Address of Grand
Master DAVIES, in saying that it was "a clear, business-like document-devoid of
all rhetorical flourish." While commending generally the reports and action of our
Grand Lodge, Bro. SCOT- argues at some length, but in a most fraternal spirit, against
our regulation adopted in that year, and reaffirmed by a decided vote in 1870, which
reads as follows :·
Resolved, That no Lodge in this jurisdiction shall bury with Masonic honors any
Mason who has committed suicide.
Our brother thinks this rule too stringent and harsh, though conceding the ablllty
and weight of the arguments of our committee that reported the resolution. As we
approved and supported the adoption of this resolution in Grand Lodge, andfare •
still decidedly in favor of its retention, we venture to say a word or two, not so much
in answer tci·Bro. ScoT, as in vindication of the policy. Were this, then, a declara ...
tion, in any shape, of an opinion as to the future reward or punishment of one who
commits suicide, we would oppose its adoption in a Masonic Lodge as soon as if it
were a definition of one of the dispnted opinions in theology. In the case of wilful,
because admittedly rational, suicides, few will differ from us in the expression of the'
decided opinion that the nse of our Masonic burial service, and especially the Grand
Honors accompanying the same, is little short of mockery, and tends to bring our
whole Order Into just and merited contempt. We are aware that some Masonsand others, so far as this matter is concerned-believe, or at least argue, that all .
suicides are insane, because the act of taking one's life is of itself an indubitable
evidence of insanity. We cannot agree to this, and think the argument of our Com·
mittee on Masonic Jurisprudence perfectly concltISive against the theory. It con·
stantly leads to the reductio ad absurdum, and is therefore unsound from the start.

Al~ this may and should be done, as would be the case were the deoeased but :

4.th. Last, but not least, the lneftl.clency and ignorance of Masonic officers in the
State are fruitful sources of immorality and want'9nness. Where officers assume the
right to profane Ood's name as a matter of personal liberty, what are we to expect
of private members, especially young men just entering the Fraternity? When
Masters of Lodges claim the right to be Intemperate, oan we be surprised that mcm·
bers get drunk and Abed blood?
·
None of the above causes authorize the brethren in forsaking the landmarks our
fathers have set. We should remember that God lives and rules. My brethren, be·
hold the sun as it rises in the east. It.beautifies and lights up the world, when at its
meridian heiii;ht; and look upop it again at close of day, as it plunges beneath the
horizon into the golden, deep, unknown west. We see no change, no variation from
dRy to day, or from year to year. This same s1m smiled upon Adam and lighted up
all the paths of Methusaleh. The moon, also, waxes and wanes With the recurring
months. Mason• are taught to draw lessons from these observations of the heavenly
orjJs. They teachus uniformity, regularity, and constancy in good works, and to go
forward under clouds and i\brightest day, in the discharge of every duty.

ing as expressive of the sense of this Grand Body:The dignity of character which marked Grand Master T. S. GATHRIGHT's entrance
upon the duties of the Grand Master of Masons or the dtate of Mississippi~the

time-honored institution, made manifest in ah his otllcial acts, have both endeared

cardinal virtues-Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence C\nd Justice. The high esteem
in which he is held by his brethren, was most warmly expressed in his being called
for two successive years to the"~ame honorable yet responsible position.
His addresses to this Grand Body are rich 10 MaRonic lore, and have been pronounced by neighboring Grand Lodges and competent judges as able Masonic doco·

truth.

Abstract of Deoislons.
1. .A 'MaAon cannot be expelled for non-payment of dues.
2. .A oandidate cannot be advanoed from one degree to another In the face of
objeotloua by a member.
3. .A member cannot disclose bis ballot, and If he does, the rejection for Initiation
at!ll stands for twelve montb1.
4.. No member can be deprived of his right to vote, or other privileges, without
a fair trial. Such action Is In direct violation of the resolutions adopted by tbll
Grand Lodge in 1867. .
•
5. All By-!,awa which suspend a member after a certain time for non·pay~ent of
dues, without a trial, are IJJegal and void.
6. .A member cannot dlmlt at 11 speolal meeting.
.
7. It is the duty of the Worshipful Master to fill all positions in the Lodge which
are made by appomtment.
8. It is proper to withdraw a petition of one totally disqualified to receive the
mysteries of Masonry, as all such petitions are ipso facto nnfl and void.
9. Ballots must be bad on all petitions, whether the committee report favorably
or unfavor11bly.
10. It requires the unanimous consent of all the members present to grant another
Lodge the privilege to confer de~ree&, or to waive jurisdiction.
11. Officers elect cannot be metalled by proxy.
12. A member has the right to object to the introduction of a visitor.
13. Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts must be re-examined each time they
apply after rejection.
14.. All rejected applicants for membership must file 11 new petition before
another ballot.
16. A Lodge oan adopt a by-law raising Its scale of dues without first obtaining
the approval of the Grand Lodge.
16. No one Is entitled to the title of an aotnal Put Master who bas not been
duly elected and Installed as Master of a chartered Lodge.
17. The deolslons of a Grand Master are not valid, after being reported to the
Grand Lodge, unless confirmed by the Grand Lodge.
18. It Is competent for a Lodge to try its m;mbera, Irrespective of any legal pro·
cedure that may be at the time pending.
19. Master Masons raised in I,odges In this jn1lsdlotlon are tpso facto members
without futther ballot, except where the work bas been done for another Lodge ;
then the brnther 1s a member of the Lodge which made the request.
20. Every resident member should be summoned, to attend trials.

T11n Report of the Committee on Correspondence was submitted by the Grand
lltoretary. It is an elaborate and very able review of the proceedings of forty
Clr111u\ Lodges, and takes up fully one-half of the entire journal of proceedings.
Wo do not think, however, that our Nevada brethren voted it to be one page too
long. The California proceedinp, of 1868, receive an appropriate and, generally,
highly commendatory ,notice. This Is titting, for the daughter should be lenient
towards the faults of the mother, even though they be quite manifest. Of the
Address of the Grand Orator, Bro. FELTON, Bro. VAN BoKKELEN says "It con·
talus many beautiful ideas, well expressed, and not hidden by an ocean of words."
Al to our decision on the subject of the burial of Ma.sonic suicides, the brother
was at first disposed to ,think that our action was too harsh, but subsequent retlec·
tlon brought bim to the conclusion that our resolution was materially correct. We
have had our say about this matter elsewhere. We doff our professional beaver at
the very flattering notice taken of our own first effort in this line of t hat year, and
for his opinion that much of which we then wrote was worthy material for his edito·
rial Masonic scissors. We a.re glad to inform our worthy brother that we are already
a convert to the Nevada theory and practice of demanding no fee for affiliation.
Bro.VAN BOKKEL~ is severe, but only justly so, In. our estimation, in his comments upon the action of the Grand Lodge of Kansas In granting a charter to the
Mount Moriah Lodge of Salt Lake City, after the application had been refused by
Nevada, and for good cause. We have read the sophistical pleadings of the Grand
Master of Kansas, and of the committee of their Grand Lodge, but can come to no
other conclusion than this, that in equity, if not in law, they committed a Ma.sonic outrage upon the rights of Nevada. We are quite sure that CalifQrhia would not have

Abstract of De~ions.
1. An officer of a Lodge, duly elected and installed, cannot resign.
2. The election of officers in a subordinate Lodge must be by ballot.
3. The examination of a visiting brother may be made by the Master, at snoh. time
and place as he may select. It need not take place in the Lodge or ante-room.
4. A committee of investigation of charges of nnmasonic conduct is not obliged
to express an opinion as to the guilt or innocence of the accused.
5. It is not the duty of a Lodge to procure counsel for an accused brother.
6. A petition for the degrees of Masonry must be ~lgned by the candidate, and any
aotlon that a Lodge may take upon a petition by other than the ap11llcant is null and
void.
7. A subordinate Lodge has the power to expel a member from all the rights and
privileges of Masonry, without the concurrence of the Grand Lodge.
8. An expelled member, in accordance with the practice in this jurisdiction, can
be fully restored without the consent of the Grand Lodge.

OHIO.
The sixtieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge ef Ohio was held In the
city of Cleveland, October 19, 1869, the M.'. w.·. HOWARD MATTHEWS, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.·. JOHN D. CALDWELL being Grand Secretary. Repre·
sentatives were present from two hundred and twenty·ftve Lodges.
The Address of Grand MaRter MATTHEWS occupies some twelve pages of the
pamphlet before us, and is a well written, bnsiness·like document, mainly devoted to.
the local alfalrs and interests of that large and important jurisdiction. He had granted
dispensations for tlte institution of fourteen new Lodges, and referred the appllca-,
tions for five others to the Grand Lodge. He says " there is stlll a strong desire to
increase the number of Lodges, without a proper regard to the real wants of the
Fraternity; and I trust that your wisdom may devise some plan to check the evil•"
A word of caution that it will not hurt other jurisdictions to heed. Several pages of
this address are devoted to a report of the cases of discipline which had come before
the Grand Master during the year, with his action thereon. One of these cases is so
unique, aod yet, in our humble estimation, so important, that we quote what the
Grand Master says at length. Does not common sense, and a due regard for the
prejudices, even, if they rnay so be called, of thousands of our brethren, require
that at least so much unmasonic work should be left undone ?Hil.vin" been informed that - - Lodge was In the habit of conferring degrees
ou the Sabbath day, I promptly arrested the charter, recognizing the principle that
Masons, to be con~istent . with their teachings, as found in the <lreat Light , should
"remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." A short time afterwards, a committee of the Lodge was deputized to wait upon me to explain their conduct, who stated
that they had, during the years of the war, conferred degrees upon t.he Sabbath,

In another case, where the Secretary of a Lodge had been tried and found guilty

He urges upon the· Grand Lodge and Fraternity the importance of providing a

. 1. That the Grand Lodge of Ohio is in earnest, and will establish a "Home for the

2. That a " Widows and Orphans' Fund" be creRted for this purpose and that
the sum of $5 ,000 be at once placed to its credit from the General Fund of this Grand

3. Tb~ one-fifth of the annual increase of this Grand Lqdp;e be annually placed to

~· That the ~. W:. Grand Master be requested to solicit donations and contributions from every Lodge under this· jurisdiction for the above-named purpose.
These resolutions were sent to .the Committee on Ways and Means, who reported
that Resolution No. 2 would bankrupt the Grand Lodge, and so they recommended that
only the fourth resolution be adopted. And it was so done. Practically, we fear
that this wil~ be like the "play of Hamlet, with Hamlet left out"; but we sup.
pose our Ohio brethren know best about their own business. Perhaps, too, it is
· not becoming in us of this jurisdiction to comment upon the action of others as we
'
have done nothing in that line ourselves.
It a}fliears that during the year, in two localities, there had been publio diaoussions of the merits and demerits of Masonry, between Masons and their opponents.
The Grand Master censures this, and thinks (soundly, too) that the best argument
which Masons can present to the world In favor of Masonry, Is to act out its principles in their daily lives. The Grand Lodge concurred, and so do we.

too many, in our humble estimation. We still adhere to the opinion that Me.sons,
either made or advanced in a hurry, do not amount to much in the long run. They
are more apt to increase the pile of rubbish than to adorn the Me.sonic Temple. He
had also granted the request of Crescent J,odge, in California, situated near
the extreme north line of the State and southern border of Oregon, " to receive the
petitions of citizens of Oregon near that ~odge,.and out of reach of any Lodge in ·
that jurisdiction."

The Grand Master of the Order to all Foreign Masonic PotrerR:

VERY DEAR BRETHREN :-At its General Assembly on the 18th July, 1869, the
Grand Orient of !<'ranee, by acclamation, adopted the following declaration:Tbe Muons under tho jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of France, by their legal
repreAentattves In the Convention of 1809, affirmed that hum·anlty and Masonry are
ontragod when color, race, or religion suffices to prevent a profane from entering the
Masonic famtty.
At the same &eRRlon, the AHembly Invited the Grand Master of the Order to
make this declarution known to all foreign Masonic Powers, t.ogether with the
resolution already taken by the Grand Orient of France to break off all alliance
with every Masonic Power which doeB not adhere to it.
In conformity with this decision, very dear brethren, I have the honor to call
your attention to this declaration. You will find in t.he Ofllcial Bulletin, which has
already been sent to you, (for July, 1869, pages SOI to S06), the motives which have
induced the Grand Orient of France to adopt It, and the sentiments which have
animated that body In this case.
I feel &•sured that this declaration will flnd uo adversary among the Grand

principles of Masonry and the natural application of its motto-Liberty, Equality,
Fraternity?
•
May I not, then, very dear brethren; count upon receiving, with the acknowledg·
ment of the receipt of this communication, the adhesion to the sentiments expressed
therein of the most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California.
I would be much obliged for an answer before the month of May, 1870-the time
of our next General Assembly.
Accept, very dear brethren, the assurance of my high consideration and of my
most fraternal Bentiments.
MELLINET,
Grand Master.
ALFRED BLANO,
Ass't Gr. MIUUr.

established June 19, I813, under

and for some years later.
A steady current of immigration, from Europe as well as from the Nort.hem
States, brought with it brethren made nuder ditfereot systems, who naturally
preferred the rite nuder which they had been initiated. This began to exercise ao
lofluence on the work of the Lodges, un.til at last a few Lodges worked either the
Scotch or French Rite exclusively, as they do at the present day. But there were
then, as now, brethren who thought nothing Masonry but the rite to which they
belonged; and, as the charters were granted to" Ancient York Masons," the legal·
ity of a Lodge working either of ·the other rites began to be questioned. To obviate
this, on the 15th of October, 1832, the Grand Lodge adopted a new constitution, by
which the cumulation (or confederation) of rites was established, together with a
sub-government for their administration, calle·d "Symbolic Chambers "-one for each
rite. The regulations were ordered to be enforced from December 1, 1832, and the
Grand Lodge completed the organization of the "Symbolic Chambers of Rites " on
the 22d of the same mouth.

GRAND LODGE ALPlNA, SWITZERLAND.-The internal affairs' of this Grand
.Lodge are r epresented to be in a satisfactory condltloo, but on account of political
and other troubles the Lodge at Liestal had suspended its labors. A portion of the
Lodges are located in an ultra Catholic population, and the Lodges of Zurich, Bern,
and Aarau, in the canton of Luzerne, have agreed to notify each other of the recep'.
tion of petitions from candidates for initiation, In order that none but well-known
citizens may gain admission into the ranks of the Fraternity and thus in some meas·
ure avoid persecution.
The Grand Lodge recognizes only the three symbolic de~rees ; the Lodges work
the A. and A. Rite, and there Is no other governing Masomc body In the jurisdic·
tion. There are twenty-eight Lodges with a membership of 1713. The membership
of the Lodges is very select, being composed of material far superior to that geq·
eraUy found in Lodges on the Continent, and they are endeavoring to keep oar inst!·
tution free from all contaminating influences.
The seat of the Grand Lodge changes with the residence of the Grand Master,
who is elected for six years. Bro. J. J. Ruwo, of Aarau, was elected Grand Master
in August, 1868, and Bro. AIME HUMBERT Grand Master Adjnnct. The latter is Direc·
tor of the Academy at Neuchatel. He Is one of the most learned and prominent
men in Switzerland, and was sent by his government to negotiate a treaty with
Japan. French is the langnage generally spoken, but Bro. HUMBERT understands
English. Our correspondent informs us that the Grand Lodge is anxious to enter
into fraternal correspondence with the American Grand Bodies.
ITALY.-The Grand Council of Symbolic Masonry at Milan has nnited with the
Grand Orient of Italy, at Florence. The other Grand Bodies still maintain an inde.
pendent existence, ind, as they entertain )Jut little fraternal feeling towards each
each other, the prospect for Masonic unity is not encouraging. We have received
the ·•Bollettino" of the Grand Orient of Italy, at Floreuce, from September, 1867, to
May, 1869. In it we find nothing to change the opinion we formerly expressed in
regard to this self-constituted body, whicn has not only invaded the jurisdiction of
friendly Masonic Powers by granting charters to Lodges composed of expelled and
unworthy Masons in the cities of Buenos Ayres and Montevideo, bot has also reco~­
nlzed and granted mutual representation to the spurious Supreme Council of this
city. By a persistent course of solicitation it has managed to obtain recognition

Yesterday I advised you that certain cases of irregularity and confusion would be
made the subject of a special report to you this morning. That report I now present,
setting before you in detail all the material facts of. each case, and di~c~osin~ all my acts
in the premises, together with a decided eii:press1on of my own opm1ons m reference

Boon after the clo~e of our last 001Dm11nication, application was made by several
brethren, residing at South Sao Diego, for a dispensation for a new Lodge at that
point. This appears to be a rival town. three miles and a half distant from the old
town of San Diego, where 'San Diego Lodge, No. 36, Is now located. The petition
was denied, for reasons which were set forth at length In the correspondence, and the
brethren were advised that they would best manifest their zeal for Mil:sonry by uniting
themselves wi ih the eii:iRting Lodge, which was feeble In numbers and tlna~es,
while it was accessible enoug'h to furnish them every Lodge privilege and enjoyment
without auy serious hardships. The suggestion was added, incidentally, that if
their representations were correct as to the growth of the new and the decay or the
old town, eventually they might reasonably ask for the removal of San J>iego:
Lodge to the new town ; but that many years must transpire before there could be
any occasion fo~ a second Lodge. The brethren seem to have acted upon this sug·
gestion rather more promptly than was anticipated ; for, at a stated meet\llg of San
Diego Lodge, he!~ very soon thereafter, without notice, and by a bare majotity, a
resolution was adopted to remove the Lodge to the new town. The old inembers,
residing mostly at the old town, feeling aggrieved, called upon me to interdict the
removal . A hasty examination revealed the fact that the charter of the Lodge was
one of the early forms in use here, and by ih express terms permitted the Ledge to
be held at San Diego, or any point within five miles thereof. Under these clrcum·
stances I declined to interfere, eii:cept to address a fraternal letter to the Master of
the Lodge, eii:pressing my disapprobation of the manner In which the vote for
removal seemed to have been taken, and advising him to remove·all ground of com·
plaint by 1ubmlttlng the measµre, before carrying it into effect, to' another vote of his
1,od1e 1 al'tor ono month's notice thereof. This course, I am sorry to say, was not
11dopt1cl I 11n1l tho removal of the Lodge was at once effected, in pursuance of the
v11t1 1lr111ly t11kon. Thereupon live or the members preferred charges against the
M11.11&1r, 11ttlnjf forth many dl1tlnct oft'enses, all which, however, were part and
p1rool or tho main act or remnvlng the Lodge. It was perfectly patent to my mind
that the trial or the Master on those charges, many of which were trivial, would only
111r1v11te the existing trouble and completely destroy the little remaining peace
and harmony of the Lodge ; while it was equally obvious that the ch11rges were In
Home measure inspired by a feeling (unconsciously, no doubt) of rivalry and chagrin.
ln this condition of affairs I took the responsibility of declining to appoint a commis·
slon . to try tbe charges, and suggested that if the b[ethren felt aggrieved by my
course, the whole matter should be laid before the Grand Lodge. Some months
have passed since, and nothing further has been heard of the matter at this office. I
·am fully persuaded that the Lodge has been saved by adopting the course I did, and I
hope that it may meet your approbation, though It was, In appearance, perhaps, rather
an arbitrary exercise of power. All the correspondence will be cheerfully submitted
to your inspection, shoul(l you be called upou to make ally further inves~igatlon.
Early in the Masonic yelll' I was informed by a member of Gravel Range Lodge
that some very disgraceful. proceedings were there transpiring, involving a general
abuse and denunciation of this Grand Body, Its olHcers and committees, on account
of certain proceedings whicli took place here one year ago. In brief, according to
representations, the Lodge was in a state of insubordination. These accusations
were very roundly asserted, and being somewhat jealous·of the dignity of this body
while under my charge, I immediately directed the Master of the Lodge to certify to
