w.-. Grand Lodge of Oa/,ifornia :-

Your committee, to whom was referr~d the memorial of Oa/,ifornia Lodge, No. I,
relative to the imposition of tines for non-attendance at funerals, respectfully submit
the following:let. That, under the Constitution of this Grand Lodge, the onl;y penalties recognized for the violation of our laws are reprimand, suspension, and expulsion: 2d.
that, in their opinion, no legislation can be had which wi:t authorize the imposition
of tines for any cause, except by an amendment to the Constitution : and, 3d, that it is
deemed Inexpedient to propose any such amendment.
Your committee cannot., however, submit this subject to the consideration of the
Grand Lodge without expressing in the most earnest manner their condemnation of the
conduct of some of the brethren in their seeming neglect of duty in not attending
the funerals of deceased brethren.· Unless this evil be remedied, it will be the
duty of Masters of Lodges to summon the members of' their Lodges in such cases;
and willful disobedience of that i;ummons involves the penalty prescribed by the
Constitution, namely-expulsion. Your committee recommend that ' no legislative
action be had on the subject.
All which is respectfuly submitted.

7b the M. •. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal ·of Bro. GEORGll L. McDANIEL
from the action had in the charges preferred by him agaiust Bro. Lours K11sER, be·
fore Corinthian Lodge, No. 69, have had the same under consideration and report
that the proceedings at the trial were correct, save in one instance. The Master of a
Lodge is, by virtue of his office and the express provision~ of the Constitution, the
chairman of all commissions acting under order of the Lodge. Therefore, at the
conclusion of the trial, when the Commissioners were determining upon the verdict
and the sentence, it was wrong for him to retire and for them to elect a chairman ;
for Sec. 8, Art. IV, Part VI, of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, says: "After
all the testimony shall have been received. the Commissioners shall proceed to deliberate upon their verdict and sentence, with none present save themselves, the Master, and the Secretary, which last shall have no voice in the prooeedinp:s."
The charge of fraud-a serious offense, "specially when committed by a Mason
against a brother-should be folly and clearly snbstantiated by the testimony. In
this case the proof rests entirely npon a profane, whose moral status carries with it
no weight; nor is the charge sustained by the books and accounts of the brother
preferring the charge. Your oommittee therefore recommend the adoption of the
following resolution:Resolved, That the appeal of Bro. GEORGE L. McDANIEL from the action of Corinthian Lodge, No. 69, in acquitting Bro. Lours KESER, be and the same is hereby dismissed.
All which is respectfully submitted.
CHARLES L. WIGGIN,
.

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of Oaliforni,a :Your committee ha.ve had under consideration the communication from Harlley
Lodge, No. 199, in which a decision is asked for upoa the question of tbe legality of
a resolution adopted, levying an assessment upon its members, and also the question upon the same subject, presented by Bro. WILLIAM 0. DAVIS.
They find nothing in the Constitution which clothes the subordinate Lodges with
power to enforce the payment of money by its members, except the provision mad·e
for the collection of monthly or quarterly dues; and the penalty for refusal or neglect in that matter is suspension. Apart from that provision, which seems to have
been intAnded to guarantee the accumulation, with certainty and regularity, of a fund
for the payment of current expenses, all else seems to have been left to the sense of
justice and spirit of fraternity by which Masons profess to be influenced in their in·
tercourse with mankind, and espeoially with e11ch other.
If tbe members of a Lodge wish to avail themselves of the coercive power in the
Constitution, let them amend their by-laws and rate their monthly dues as high as
hey deem llecessary. They can do that and see how they like it, and if they don't,
why-amend.
· All which is respectfully submitted.
GILBRRT B. CLAIBORNE, }
ABISHA SWAIN,
.

take the degrees of Masonry in that Lodge; that, at the time alleged, Progress
Lodge conferred the first degree of Masonry upon said MAGUIRE; that MAGUIRE was
at that time a resident of Vallejo, and within the jurisdictif>n of Na·u al Lodg~,No. 87;
and that MAGUIRE was maimed by having lost the last three fingers of his left band.
Your committee are clearly of the opinion that, from the time this pandldate,
MA.GUIRE, was recommended for the degrees of Masonry.until the first degree was
oonferred upon him, many of the members of Progreas Lodge were guifty of gre11t
negligence and disregard of their Masonic obligations. Neither those reclommending
him, nor those who were appointed as a committee of investigation,coulp have made
tho proper eifort to Inform themselves about MAGUmE's residence, ph~sical fitness,
or moral character. Your committee see nothing, however, in this record, implicating
Bro. JA1i1~s H. HJ.RDY, Master of Progress Lodge, in these irregular prodeedings. He
did not appoint the committee of investigation, not then being Master pf the Lodge,
and subsequently it would seem that he did all in his power to remedy the evil caused
by MAGUIRK'B admiBBion. He caused charges to be presented against MAGUIRE, and
when be was acquitted by the commission elected to try him, the ~aster at once
caused an appeal to be taken to this Grand Body.
The history of this case, as presented by the record, convinces your committee
that the judgment of the commission, declaring Progress Lodge guilty of the cha.rges
preferred and decreeing a forfeiture of its charter, is correct. They are, however,
of the opinion that the Grand Lodge should relieve all the members of that Lodge
from the suspension which followed the judgment of the forfeiture of charter, and
should direct that all who were guilty of irregularities in the matte1· upon which
were based the charges of Nava_l Lodge, No. 87, be brought to trial ther~for.
Jt would seem that only a portion of the members of Progress Lodge were in this
matter actually guilty of unmasonic conduct, and, in the opinion of your committee
only the guilty should be punished. Some of the members of that Lodge doubtles~
deserve punishment; others are good and true. Your committee therefore recommend the adoption of the following .resolutions:Resolved, That the Grand Lodge approves the judgment of the commission decree·
ing the forfeiture of the charter of Progreas Lodge, No. 125, and that said Lodge is
hereby declared extinct.
Resolved, That tbe memb.ers of Progreaa Lodge, No. 125, be and are hereby
relieved from the suspension which the judgment of forfeiture of charter would
under our laws, entail upon them.

Bro. WrLLIAH A. DA.VIES, from the specie.I committee to whom was
referred that portion of the Grand Master's Address relative to a system
for the instruction and supervision of the Lodges, presented the following
report:To tlie M." W." Grand Lodge of (Jali,fornia :Your committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand Master's
Address recommending the creation of some system which would secure a visitation
of all the Lodges in the State by Inspectors and Deputy Grand Lecturers, who should
be qaalifiedt. not only to instraot In the ritual of Masonry, but to examine the
records of and the manner of tranS11ctiog business by the Lodges, to advise in re·
gard to the proper discharge of the various duties devolving upon their Masters, and
· to report annually to the Grand Master and Gran!l Lecturer the general condition of
the Lodges which might be assigned to their supervision, report as follows:The committee have entered upon the duty assigned them with a full conviction
of the necessity for the adoption of some system of inspection of the Lodges of the
jurisdiction which would result in the correction of the many irregularities so plainly
set forth by the Grand Master, as well as insure the result aimed at by the Grand
Lodge in adopting, and making obligatory upon its subordinates, the practice of the
uniform work established fifteen years ago, revised and reaffirmed six years ago, and
exemplified during the present session.
This question of the importance of a general visitation of the Lodges in order to
secure uniformity of work is not a new one, it having occupied the attention of the

IH70. J.

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

439

Cl111n1t 1.odge as early as 1851. Grand Master STEVENSON then called the attention
11r U1l11 body to its importance, and a committee was appointed who recommended
1111 ' rt1tlon of districts and the appointment of Lecturers to secure such visitation.
In II • • Bros. JOHN R. CRANDALL and lsAA.C DAVIS set forth, in a report on this sub1• t, thu Importance of 11 general visitation, and recommended the appointment or
l1tol11rorR for that purpose. In 1865 the Grand Lodge adopted the work as exem·
pllnn1I at the present session, making it obligatory upon the Lodges, and your com·
n1lltoo congratulate this Grand Lodge upon the result of its action at that time.
ln1too.d or confusion and disagreement as to which of the many ditferent rituals in
1110 was the correct one, we now have bat the contention, or rather emulation, of
who oan best work the work or this jurisdiction. Our Lodges are opened and closed
allke.-our modes of recognition are given and received in the same manner-our
lectures and obligations are the same in San Francisco, Sacramento, Siskiyou, and
Ban Diego. With a foundation so laid, it is l>nt necessary that the Grand Lodge
1hould adopt some plan by 'which the advantages of Instruction that h&ve produced
this result in the populous and conveniently located counties of the State, should
be shared by those remotely situated. To secure this, we must provide for an annual
visitation of all ; and this we think can only be secured by dividing the State Into
convenient districts. At the Bllme time your committee feel that the expens&
attending the adoption of any system (either to the Grand Lodge or to the suhordl·
nates) is something that should be well considered before the change should be made,
by your order, the law ofthisjnrisdicti!)n. Their aim, therefore, has been to present
the 1implest plan which it was believed would accomplish the result desired by the
Grand Muter, and would be of most real benefit to the Lodges, with, to them, the
leut co1t. Your committee believe that, if this plan be approved, and the Grand
H111ter be fortunate In 1eouring the services of brethren as Inspectors or the several
dl1trlct1, not only qualified to teach the ritual, bnt competent to advise the Master
lntelltgently in reg11rd to the requirements of his office-to examine the records of
the Lodge and point out any Irregularities in its proceedings-to correct those of
lesser Importance and report to the Grand Master such as demand the attention
ot the executive head-there can be no doubt that It· would be of the greateet
poBSlble benefit to 11 majority of our Lodges.

The Grand Secretary preaented certain questions submitted for the conaideration of the Grand Lodge by Mr. P. ANDERSON; which were referred
to the Standing Committee on Jurisprudence.
He also presented the credentials of Bro. LAWRENCE CONLY OWEN, as
the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Nebraska near the Grand Lodge
of California, and the several credentials of ·Bro. ALEXANDER GURDON
ABELL, as Representative, near this Grand Lodge, of the Grand Lodges of
Florida, Kentucky, Mississippi, Oregon, and Tennessee; and, upon his
motion, those brethren were received and duly accredited in that honorable
capacity.
The Grand Secretary reported that the order o~e Grand Lodge, at its
last Annnal Communication, directing him to procure the portrait of the
.M:. W. ·. CHARLES MARSH, Past Grand Master, bad been complied with, and
that the portrait was now hanging in its appropriate place in the gallery set
apart for that purpose.
He also reported that the duty assigned to the elective Grand Officers,
at the last Annual Col)'.lmunication, viz.-tbat of" devising and procuring
a suitable testimonial for presentation" to the M. '. W.-. CHARLES MARSH,
Past Grand Master, had been performed; whereupon the Grand Stewards
opened, and placed upon a table in front of the pedestal, the handsome
chest containing the several pieces of silver comprising that token of the
respect and esteem of the Grand Lodge for its late chief officer, and, Bro.
MARSH being present, the Grand Master addressed him as follows : MosT WORSHIPFUL SIR AND BROTHER:You will remember that, at the close of oor last Aoooal Commooicatioo, the
elective Grand Officers were directed, by a resolution of the Grand Lodge, to pro·
cure for you some fitting testimonial of its esteem and regard. They have performed
that .pleasant duty, and in these six pieces of silver you behold the choice which
they have made. On this principal piece, in order that, so long as it may endure in
your hands or lo the hands of your posterity, there may be no mistaking the source
and occasion of the compliment paid you, they have caused this Inscription to be
placed: "To the M.'.
CHARLES M.tRSB, Past Grand Master,thls,'with five accom·
paoyiog piec.es of silver, was presented by the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of Ci>llfornia, at its Aoooal Commoolcatioo lo October, A. L.
5870, as an evidence of its just appreciation of his long, faithful, and usefal services
in that body.''
These few words are in themselves a perfect history, and, as to you they must
ever be more grateful than the loftiest panegyric whicb could be anywhere else pronounced, I esteem myself peculiarly fortunate that Tam·the representative and 11er·
vaot of the Grand Lodge in presenting to yon these well-earned tokens. In all my
Masonic service and experience I have never welc0med a duty with more pleasure

BRETHREN : I thankfully accept this gift, not alone from the fact that it is to me a
